recipes.title: Traditional Sbrinz (Swiss)
recipes.source_note: Sbrinz is one of Switzerland's oldest and hardest cheeses, possibly predating Parmesan. It was a major trade item through the Gotthard Pass and may have influenced the development of Italian grana cheeses.
recipes.description: Switzerland's ancient hard cheese, intensely flavored and crystalline - historically traded across the Alps and possibly the ancestor of Parmesan.

instructions.text: Heat raw milk to 90°F.
Add starter culture and ripen for 20 minutes.
Add diluted rennet, stir gently. Let set 25-30 minutes until clean break.
Cut curd into rice-sized grains (very small). Let rest 5 minutes.
Slowly raise temperature to 135°F over 40 minutes while stirring constantly.
Hold at 135°F for 45-60 minutes, stirring, until curds are very firm.
Gather curds in cloth and press under whey briefly.
Transfer to mold and press at 50 lbs immediately.
Press at increasing weights up to 100 lbs over 24 hours with multiple flips.
Brine for 3-4 weeks, turning daily (very long brining for Sbrinz).
Age at 55°F and 85% humidity for 18-36 months minimum.
Turn weekly and brush the rind during aging.

notes: Traditional Sbrinz wheels weigh 55-100 lbs - scale up for authentic results
The very long brining period (weeks vs hours) is unique to Sbrinz
Sbrinz is so hard it's traditionally broken apart rather than cut
Can be eaten in paper-thin shavings (Hobelkäse) or grated like Parmesan
Some historians believe Sbrinz was the ancestor of Italian grana cheeses

recipes.title: Traditional Jarlsberg (Norwegian Swiss-Style)
recipes.source_note: Jarlsberg was developed in the 1950s at the Agricultural University of Norway, based on a cheese made in the Jarlsberg region in the 1820s. It combines Swiss-style eye formation with a milder, nuttier flavor.
recipes.description: Norwegian Swiss-style cheese with large eyes, sweet nutty flavor, and excellent melting properties - Norway's most famous cheese export.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 90°F. Add calcium chloride if using pasteurized milk.
Add both starter cultures and propionic bacteria. Stir well and ripen for 30 minutes.
Add diluted rennet, stir gently. Let set 30-40 minutes until clean break.
Cut curd into 1/4-inch cubes. Let rest 5 minutes.
Slowly raise temperature to 102°F over 30 minutes while stirring.
Remove 1/3 of whey. Replace with 102°F water (curd washing for sweeter flavor).
Raise temperature to 108°F over 15 minutes while stirring.
Let curds settle, drain whey, and transfer to mold.
Press at 10 lbs for 30 minutes. Flip and press at 30 lbs for 6 hours.
Flip and press at 50 lbs for 12 hours.
Brine for 18-24 hours in saturated salt solution.
Age at 55°F for 2 weeks, then move to 'warm room' at 68-70°F for 4-6 weeks for eye development.
Return to 55°F and age for 3-12 months total.

notes: The combination of mesophilic and thermophilic starters is key to Jarlsberg's unique flavor
The warm room phase develops the characteristic large eyes (holes)
Jarlsberg is sweeter and milder than Swiss Emmental due to curd washing
Eyes should be round, smooth, and evenly distributed

recipes.title: Traditional Danablu (Danish Blue)
recipes.source_note: Danish Blue was developed in the early 1920s by Marius Boel as a Danish alternative to Roquefort. It quickly became Denmark's most famous blue cheese, known for its creamy texture and sharp, tangy flavor.
recipes.description: Creamy, sharp Danish blue cheese developed as a Roquefort alternative - now beloved worldwide for its bold flavor and smooth texture.

instructions.text: Combine milk and cream. Heat to 86°F. Add calcium chloride if using pasteurized milk.
Add starter and P. roqueforti. Stir well and ripen for 1 hour.
Add diluted rennet, stir gently. Let set 1-1.5 hours until soft curd forms.
Cut curd into 1-inch cubes (larger for open texture). Let rest 10 minutes.
Gently stir curds for 30 minutes at 86°F. Curds should remain soft.
Drain whey and ladle curds into cylindrical molds. Do not press.
Let drain at room temperature for 24 hours, flipping every 6-8 hours.
Unmold and salt all surfaces heavily. Repeat salting over 3-4 days.
Transfer to aging cave at 50°F and 95% humidity.
After 1 week, pierce the cheese thoroughly with sterilized needles.
Age for 8-12 weeks, turning weekly. Blue veins should develop within 3-4 weeks of piercing.

notes: Danish Blue is creamier than Roquefort because it uses cow's milk plus cream
Homogenized milk produces a creamier, more spreadable cheese
Heavy salting is traditional and contributes to the sharp flavor
The piercing allows air to reach the interior for blue mold growth

recipes.title: Traditional Cantal (Auvergne)
recipes.source_note: Cantal is one of the oldest French cheeses, mentioned by Pliny the Elder in the 1st century AD. Made in the volcanic Auvergne region, it may be the ancestor of many European cheeses including English cheddar.
recipes.description: Ancient French cheese from the volcanic Auvergne, possibly the ancestor of cheddar - with a complex, buttery flavor that deepens with age.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 90°F.
Add starter culture, stir well, and ripen for 1 hour.
Add diluted rennet, stir gently. Let set 45-60 minutes until clean break.
Cut curd into 1/2-inch cubes. Let rest 5 minutes.
Slowly raise temperature to 95°F over 30 minutes while stirring gently.
Drain whey. Press curds lightly in mold for 1 hour.
Remove and break up the pressed curd. Let rest covered for 8-12 hours (the 'tome' stage).
Break the tome into walnut-sized pieces. This double-handling is unique to Cantal.
Mix in salt thoroughly.
Pack salted curds into mold. Press at 30 lbs for 2 hours.
Flip and press at 50 lbs for 24 hours.
Age at 50°F and 95% humidity. Cantal Jeune: 1-2 months; Entre-Deux: 3-6 months; Vieux: 8+ months.

notes: The 'tome' stage (resting broken curds) is unique to Cantal and gives it distinctive texture
Cantal Jeune (young) is mild and supple; Vieux (old) is firm, crumbly, and intense
Some historians believe Cantal is the ancestor of English cheddar

recipes.title: Traditional Morbier (Jura)
recipes.source_note: Morbier originated in Franche-Comté when farmers making Comté would protect leftover evening curd with ash, then add morning curd on top. The ash line became its signature, even though it's now purely decorative.
recipes.description: French cheese with a distinctive black ash line, originally a frugal farmhouse creation using leftover Comté curds.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 90°F. Add calcium chloride if using pasteurized milk.
Add starter culture, stir well, and ripen for 30 minutes.
Add diluted rennet, stir gently. Let set 30-40 minutes until clean break.
Cut curd into 1/2-inch cubes. Let rest 5 minutes.
Slowly raise temperature to 100°F over 30 minutes while stirring.
Hold at 100°F for 20 minutes, stirring gently.
Drain whey and divide curds in half.
Press the first half of curds lightly into the mold.
Sprinkle vegetable ash evenly over the surface of the pressed curds.
Add the remaining curds on top of the ash layer.
Press at 10 lbs for 30 minutes. Flip and press at 20 lbs for 8 hours.
Salt the surface and let dry for 24 hours.
Age at 55°F and 90% humidity for 2-3 months, turning weekly and wiping with brine if needed.

notes: The ash line was originally functional (protecting overnight curds) but is now decorative
Traditional Morbier used soot from the wooden vat; modern versions use vegetable ash
The cheese should be semi-soft with a fruity, slightly bitter flavor
The rind develops a gray-brown color naturally during aging

recipes.title: Traditional Saint-Nectaire (Auvergne)
recipes.source_note: Saint-Nectaire has been made in the volcanic highlands of Auvergne since at least the 17th century. Named after Marshal Henri de la Ferté-Senneterre who introduced it to Louis XIV's court, it's prized for its rich, earthy flavor.
recipes.description: Earthy Auvergnat cheese with a complex, mushroomy rind and creamy interior - a favorite of Louis XIV.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 90°F.
Add starter culture, stir well, and ripen for 30 minutes.
Add diluted rennet, stir gently. Let set 45 minutes until clean break.
Cut curd into 1/2-inch cubes. Let rest 5 minutes.
Stir gently for 10 minutes while maintaining 90°F.
Raise temperature slowly to 95°F over 20 minutes while stirring.
Drain whey and transfer curds to flat round molds.
Press lightly at 5 lbs for 2 hours, flipping several times.
Press at 15 lbs for 8-12 hours.
Salt all surfaces and let dry for 24 hours.
Age on rye straw (traditional) at 50°F and 95% humidity for 4-8 weeks.
Turn daily and wipe with brine as needed. A fuzzy gray-brown rind with orange patches should develop.

notes: Traditional Saint-Nectaire is aged on rye straw, which contributes to the flavor and rind development
The rind should be fuzzy with gray, brown, and orange molds - this is normal
Fermier (farmhouse) Saint-Nectaire has an oval green casein mark; laitier (dairy) has a square mark
The paste should be creamy and slightly bulging when ripe

recipes.title: Traditional Stracchino/Crescenza (Lombardy)
recipes.source_note: Stracchino (also called Crescenza) has been made in Lombardy since at least the Middle Ages. The name comes from 'stracca' (tired) - referring to tired cows descending from Alpine pastures whose milk made the best cheese.
recipes.description: Soft, spreadable Italian cheese with a mild, milky flavor - named for the 'tired' cows whose rich autumn milk made the best wheels.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 100°F. Add calcium chloride if using pasteurized milk.
Add starter culture, stir well, and ripen for 20 minutes.
Add diluted rennet (very small amount), stir gently. Let set 30-45 minutes until soft curd.
Cut curd into 1-inch cubes. Let rest 10 minutes.
Very gently stir curds for 10 minutes while maintaining 100°F.
Drain whey gently and ladle curds into square molds without pressing.
Let drain at room temperature for 8-12 hours, flipping every 2-3 hours.
Unmold and salt lightly all surfaces.
Refrigerate immediately. Stracchino is ready to eat in 1-3 days.
Use within 1-2 weeks; it does not age well.

notes: Stracchino is meant to be eaten very fresh - it's not an aged cheese
The texture should be soft and spreadable, like a thickened cream cheese
Traditional in northern Italian focaccia (focaccia di Recco) and as a spread
Crescenza is the same cheese with slightly more acid development

recipes.title: Traditional Vacherin Mont d'Or (Swiss/French)
recipes.source_note: Vacherin Mont d'Or has been made in the Jura Mountains since at least the 18th century. It's a seasonal cheese, produced only from late August to March when there isn't enough milk for Gruyère production.
recipes.description: Luxurious seasonal cheese wrapped in spruce bark, so soft it's eaten with a spoon - a winter delicacy from the Jura Mountains.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 86°F.
Add starter culture and ripen for 30 minutes.
Add diluted rennet, stir gently. Let set 45-60 minutes until soft curd.
Cut curd into 3/4-inch cubes. Let rest 10 minutes.
Stir gently for 20 minutes at 86°F.
Drain whey and ladle curds into round molds.
Let drain at room temperature for 12-24 hours, flipping every 4-6 hours.
Salt all surfaces and let dry for 24 hours.
Wrap the cheese with soaked spruce bark, securing with a wooden band.
Place in a spruce wood box slightly larger than the cheese.
Age at 55°F and 95% humidity for 3-4 weeks, turning daily and wiping with brine.
When ripe, the cheese should bulge slightly and feel liquid under the rind.

notes: The spruce bark is essential - it gives Vacherin its distinctive resinous aroma
When perfectly ripe, cut off the top rind and eat the cheese with a spoon
Traditional to bake in oven (350°F for 20 minutes) and dip bread and potatoes
Both Swiss and French versions exist; Swiss is slightly larger

recipes.title: Traditional Livarot (Normandy)
recipes.source_note: Livarot has been made in the Pays d'Auge region of Normandy since at least the 13th century. Called 'The Colonel' due to the five strips of reed or paper wrapped around it (resembling military stripes), it's one of Normandy's great washed-rind cheeses.
recipes.description: Pungent Norman cheese nicknamed 'The Colonel' for its distinctive reed bands - one of France's oldest and most flavorful washed-rind cheeses.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 90°F. Add calcium chloride if using pasteurized milk. Add annatto for color.
Add starter and B. linens. Ripen for 1 hour.
Add diluted rennet, stir gently. Let set 1 hour until soft curd.
Cut curd into 1/2-inch cubes. Let rest 10 minutes.
Stir gently for 20 minutes at 90°F.
Drain whey and ladle curds into cylindrical molds.
Let drain at room temperature for 24-36 hours, flipping every 6-8 hours.
Unmold and salt all surfaces. Let dry for 24 hours.
Transfer to aging cave at 55°F and 95% humidity.
Wash with brine (sometimes with annatto added for color) 3 times per week for 6-8 weeks.
After 3-4 weeks, wrap with 5 bands of reed or paper around the circumference.
Continue aging until rind is sticky orange-red and interior is soft.

notes: The five bands (laîches) give Livarot its 'Colonel' nickname
Traditional Livarot was made from partially skimmed milk after cream was taken for butter
The orange-red rind comes from annatto added to the wash
Extremely pungent when ripe - one of the strongest Norman cheeses

recipes.title: Traditional Maroilles (Picardy)
recipes.source_note: Maroilles was created at the Maroilles Abbey in northern France around 962 AD by Benedictine monks. It's one of France's oldest and most pungent washed-rind cheeses.
recipes.description: Ancient monastic cheese with an intensely pungent washed rind - created by Benedictine monks over a thousand years ago.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 86°F. Add calcium chloride if using pasteurized milk.
Add starter and B. linens. Ripen for 1 hour.
Add diluted rennet, stir gently. Let set 1-1.5 hours until soft curd.
Cut curd into 1/2-inch cubes. Let rest 15 minutes.
Stir gently for 30 minutes at 86°F.
Drain whey and ladle curds into square molds (traditional shape).
Let drain at room temperature for 48 hours, flipping every 8-12 hours.
Unmold and salt heavily. Let dry for 48 hours.
Transfer to humid cave at 55°F and 95% humidity.
Wash with beer or cider mixed with brine every 2-3 days for 2-4 months.
The rind should develop a shiny, sticky, brick-red surface.

notes: Maroilles is traditionally square - make sure to use square molds
The beer/cider wash is traditional in this region and adds to the complexity
One of the strongest-smelling cheeses in France - but the flavor is milder than the aroma
Essential ingredient in Flamiche au Maroilles (Belgian/French cheese tart)

recipes.title: Traditional Bleu d'Auvergne
recipes.source_note: Bleu d'Auvergne was invented around 1854 by Antoine Roussel, a farmer who experimented with introducing rye bread mold into his cheese. It quickly became popular and received AOC protection in 1975.
recipes.description: Creamy French blue cheese from volcanic Auvergne, created by a curious farmer's experiment with rye bread mold.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 86°F. Add calcium chloride if using pasteurized milk.
Add starter and P. roqueforti. Stir well and ripen for 1 hour.
Add diluted rennet, stir gently. Let set 1-1.5 hours until soft curd.
Cut curd into 1-inch cubes (large for blue cheese). Let rest 15 minutes.
Stir gently for 30 minutes at 86°F.
Drain whey and ladle curds loosely into cylindrical molds. Do not press.
Let drain at room temperature for 24-48 hours, flipping every 8-12 hours.
Unmold and salt all surfaces heavily over 3-4 days.
Transfer to aging cave at 45-50°F and 95% humidity.
After 10 days, pierce the cheese with sterilized skewers (20-30 holes).
Age for 4-8 weeks, turning weekly. Blue veins should develop within 2-3 weeks of piercing.

notes: Bleu d'Auvergne is creamier and milder than Roquefort
The piercing allows oxygen to reach the interior for blue mold growth
Traditional aging was in the natural caves of the Auvergne volcanic region
Pairs well with sweet wines like Sauternes

recipes.title: Traditional Fourme d'Ambert
recipes.source_note: Fourme d'Ambert is one of France's oldest blue cheeses, possibly dating to Roman times. The tall cylindrical shape ('fourme') is traditional to the Auvergne region. It's milder than other blues, making it a good introduction to blue cheese.
recipes.description: Ancient Auvergnat blue in a distinctive tall cylinder, milder and creamier than most blues - possibly dating to Roman times.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 90°F. Add calcium chloride if using pasteurized milk.
Add starter and P. roqueforti. Stir well and ripen for 30 minutes.
Add diluted rennet, stir gently. Let set 1 hour until soft curd.
Cut curd into 1-inch cubes. Let rest 10 minutes.
Stir gently for 20 minutes at 90°F.
Drain most whey. Ladle curds into tall cylindrical molds (the distinctive 'fourme' shape).
Let drain at room temperature for 24-48 hours, flipping every 8-12 hours.
Unmold and dry salt over 3-4 days.
Transfer to aging cave at 50°F and 95% humidity.
After 1 week, pierce with needles horizontally (the tall shape requires horizontal piercing).
Age for 4-8 weeks until blue-green veins develop throughout.

notes: The tall cylindrical shape is traditional - use appropriate molds
Fourme d'Ambert is one of the mildest French blue cheeses
The gray rind is natural and edible but can be removed if desired
Often paired with pears, walnuts, and sweet wines

recipes.title: Traditional Banon (Provençal Leaf-Wrapped)
recipes.source_note: Banon cheese has been made in the hills of Haute-Provence for centuries, traditionally wrapped in chestnut leaves tied with raffia. The Roman emperor Antoninus Pius allegedly died from eating too much at a banquet featuring a cheese from this region.
recipes.description: Provençal cheese wrapped in chestnut leaves, developing complex flavors as it ages in its leafy cocoon.

ingredients.prep_note: dried and soaked in brandy or eau-de-vie

instructions.text: Heat milk to 68-72°F (cool room temperature - Banon uses very little heat).
Add starter and stir well. Ripen for 30 minutes.
Add diluted rennet, stir gently. Let set for 12-24 hours until a soft, delicate curd forms.
Very gently ladle the fragile curd into small round molds.
Let drain at room temperature for 24-48 hours, flipping gently.
Unmold and salt lightly. Let dry for 1-2 days until surface is slightly firm.
Soak dried chestnut leaves in brandy or eau-de-vie until pliable.
Wrap each cheese in overlapping chestnut leaves, then tie securely with raffia.
Age at 55°F and 85% humidity for 2-4 weeks.
The cheese will soften and develop complex flavors from the leaves.

notes: Traditional Banon uses raw goat's milk, but some versions include sheep or cow
The chestnut leaves are traditionally dipped in marc de Provence (grape brandy)
Young Banon is mild and chalky; aged Banon becomes creamy with earthy, boozy notes
If chestnut leaves are unavailable, grape leaves can substitute

recipes.title: Traditional Tetilla (Galician)
recipes.source_note: Tetilla has been made in Galicia for centuries. Its distinctive pear or breast shape (the name means 'small breast') is traditional to the region. It's a mild, creamy cheese that pairs perfectly with Galician cuisine.
recipes.description: Distinctive pear-shaped Galician cheese with a mild, creamy flavor - its shape has been traditional for centuries.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 86°F. Add calcium chloride if using pasteurized milk.
Add starter culture, stir well, and ripen for 30 minutes.
Add diluted rennet, stir gently. Let set 30-40 minutes until clean break.
Cut curd into 1/2-inch cubes. Let rest 5 minutes.
Stir gently for 15 minutes while maintaining 86°F.
Raise temperature slowly to 95°F over 20 minutes while stirring.
Drain whey and transfer curds to tetilla-shaped molds (pear/cone shape with nipple on top).
Press lightly at 5 lbs for 2 hours, flipping once.
Press at 15 lbs for 8-12 hours.
Brine for 8-12 hours in saturated salt solution.
Air dry for 2-3 days.
Age at 50°F and 85% humidity for 2-4 weeks, turning regularly.

notes: The distinctive pear/breast shape is essential to authentic Tetilla
Traditional molds have a small nipple point at the top
Tetilla is mild, slightly tangy, and becomes more flavorful with age
Classic pairing with Galician empanadas and Albariño wine

recipes.title: Traditional Queso de Murcia al Vino (Wine-Washed)
recipes.source_note: Queso de Murcia has been made from Murciano-Granadina goat milk in southeastern Spain for centuries. The 'al vino' version is washed with local red wine, giving it a distinctive purple rind.
recipes.description: Spanish goat cheese washed with red wine, developing a striking purple rind and complex, fruity flavors.

instructions.text: Heat goat milk to 90°F. Add calcium chloride.
Add starter culture, stir well, and ripen for 30 minutes.
Add diluted rennet, stir gently. Let set 45-60 minutes until clean break.
Cut curd into 1/4-inch cubes. Let rest 5 minutes.
Slowly raise temperature to 104°F over 30 minutes while stirring.
Hold at 104°F for 30 minutes, stirring frequently.
Drain whey and transfer curds to molds.
Press at 15 lbs for 1 hour. Flip and press at 30 lbs for 8-12 hours.
Brine for 12-24 hours in saturated salt solution.
Air dry for 2-3 days.
Submerge the cheese in red wine for 48-72 hours, turning occasionally.
Age at 50°F and 85% humidity for 2-3 months, washing with wine weekly.

notes: The wine wash gives the rind its distinctive purple-red color
Traditional uses Monastrell (Mourvèdre) wine from the Jumilla region
The interior is white and firm with a clean, tangy goat flavor
The wine adds fruity notes to the rind while the paste remains pure goat

recipes.title: Traditional Kashkaval (Balkan)
recipes.source_note: Kashkaval (also Kaşar, Kasseri, Kachkawali) is a family of stretched-curd cheeses made throughout the Balkans, Turkey, and Eastern Mediterranean since ancient times. The name may derive from the Italian 'caciocavallo.'
recipes.description: Traditional Balkan pasta filata cheese, similar to provolone but with regional variations across Bulgaria, Turkey, Greece, and beyond.

instructions.text: Combine milks and heat to 95°F. Add calcium chloride if using pasteurized milk.
Add starter culture, stir well, and ripen for 45 minutes.
Add diluted rennet, stir gently. Let set 30-45 minutes until clean break.
Cut curd into 1/2-inch cubes. Let rest 5 minutes.
Slowly raise temperature to 104°F over 20 minutes while stirring.
Drain curds and let mat at 100°F for 2-3 hours until pH reaches 5.2-5.3.
Test for stretch: place a small piece in 170°F water - it should stretch smoothly.
Cut matted curd into strips. Heat water to 170°F with salt.
Stretch curd in hot water until smooth and elastic, folding repeatedly.
Form into wheel or brick shape.
Brine for 12-24 hours.
Age at 55°F and 85% humidity for 2-6 months.

notes: Kashkaval is the generic Balkan name; Kaşar is Turkish, Kasseri is Greek
Young Kashkaval is mild and sliceable; aged becomes sharp and granular
Excellent melting cheese used in traditional Balkan dishes

recipes.title: Traditional Bulgarian Sirene (White Brine Cheese)
recipes.source_note: Sirene is the traditional Bulgarian white brine cheese, similar to feta but typically made from cow or mixed milk. It's been a staple of Bulgarian cuisine for thousands of years.
recipes.description: Traditional Bulgarian brine cheese, tangy and crumbly - the foundation of Bulgarian cuisine from shopska salad to banitsa.

instructions.text: Combine milks and heat to 86°F. Add calcium chloride if using pasteurized milk.
Add starter culture, stir well, and ripen for 1 hour.
Add diluted rennet, stir gently. Let set 45-60 minutes until clean break.
Cut curd into 1/2-inch cubes. Let rest 10 minutes.
Stir gently for 20 minutes at 86°F.
Let curds settle, then drain most whey.
Ladle curds into molds or form into a block. Press lightly for 4-6 hours.
Cut the drained cheese into 3-4 inch blocks.
Make brine: dissolve salt in water (about 10% solution).
Place cheese blocks in brine and refrigerate.
Age in brine for 2-3 weeks minimum. Can store in brine for months.

notes: Sirene is traditionally made from cow's milk in Bulgaria, unlike Greek feta
Essential for shopska salad, banitsa (cheese pastry), and many Bulgarian dishes
Store submerged in brine - it will keep for months refrigerated
The longer it ages in brine, the tangier and firmer it becomes

recipes.title: Traditional Greek Graviera
recipes.source_note: Graviera is Greece's second most popular cheese after feta. The name derives from Gruyère, though Greek graviera developed independently and varies by region - Cretan graviera uses sheep's milk, Naxos uses cow's milk.
recipes.description: Greece's beloved hard cheese with nutty, sweet flavors - the island varieties are considered finest.

instructions.text: Combine milks and heat to 93°F. Add calcium chloride if using pasteurized.
Add starter culture, stir well, and ripen for 30 minutes.
Add diluted rennet, stir gently. Let set 30-40 minutes until clean break.
Cut curd into 1/4-inch cubes (small). Let rest 5 minutes.
Slowly raise temperature to 122°F over 40 minutes while stirring.
Continue stirring at 122°F for 30 minutes until curds are firm.
Drain whey and transfer curds to molds.
Press at 15 lbs for 30 minutes. Flip and press at 30 lbs for 6 hours.
Flip and press at 50 lbs for 24 hours.
Brine for 24-48 hours in saturated salt solution.
Air dry for 3-5 days.
Age at 55°F and 85% humidity for 3-8 months, turning weekly.

notes: Cretan Graviera (sheep/goat milk) is considered the finest
Naxos Graviera uses cow's milk and is milder
The high cooking temperature creates the firm, smooth texture
Excellent table cheese and for saganaki (pan-fried cheese)

recipes.title: Traditional Turkish Tulum (Goatskin Cheese)
recipes.source_note: Tulum peyniri has been made in Anatolia for millennia. 'Tulum' means goatskin - the cheese was traditionally aged in goatskin bags, which gave it a distinctive flavor and allowed shepherds to transport it.
recipes.description: Ancient Turkish cheese traditionally aged in goatskin bags, with a distinctive sharp, crumbly character.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 90°F.
Add starter culture, stir well, and ripen for 30 minutes.
Add diluted rennet, stir gently. Let set 1 hour until firm curd.
Cut curd into 1/2-inch cubes. Let rest 10 minutes.
Stir gently for 20 minutes at 90°F.
Drain whey thoroughly. Place curds in cloth and hang to drain for 24 hours.
Crumble the drained curd and mix with salt.
Traditional method: Pack salted curds tightly into a prepared goatskin bag.
Modern alternative: Pack into a ceramic crock or vacuum-seal in portions.
Age at cool room temperature (55-65°F) for 3-6 months.
The cheese should develop a crumbly, sharp character.

notes: Traditional tulum is aged in a goatskin (tulum) which imparts distinctive flavor
Modern versions use cloth or ceramic containers
The texture is crumbly like aged feta, with a sharp, complex flavor
Excellent crumbled over salads or in Turkish gözleme

recipes.title: Traditional Akkawi (Levantine)
recipes.source_note: Akkawi cheese is named after the city of Acre (Akko/Akka) in modern-day Israel, though it's been made throughout the Levant for centuries. It's a mild white brine cheese, essential for knafeh and other Middle Eastern sweets.
recipes.description: Mild Levantine brine cheese named after the city of Acre, essential for authentic knafeh and Middle Eastern cuisine.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 90°F. Add calcium chloride if using pasteurized milk.
Add starter culture (small amount for mild cheese), stir, and ripen for 15 minutes.
Add diluted rennet, stir gently. Let set 30-45 minutes until clean break.
Cut curd into 1/2-inch cubes. Let rest 5 minutes.
Stir gently for 15 minutes at 90°F.
Drain whey and transfer curds to molds.
Press lightly at 5 lbs for 2 hours.
Flip and press at 10 lbs for 4 hours.
Cut into 3-4 inch blocks.
Make brine (about 8-10% salt solution) and submerge cheese.
Store in brine for 1-2 weeks before using. Keep refrigerated.
Before using in desserts, soak in water to remove excess salt.

notes: Akkawi is intentionally mild - don't over-culture
For knafeh and sweets, soak the cheese in fresh water for several hours to remove salt
The texture should be smooth and elastic when heated
Also used in savory pastries and eaten fresh with herbs

recipes.title: Traditional Nabulsi Cheese (Palestinian)
recipes.source_note: Nabulsi cheese is named after the city of Nablus in the Palestinian West Bank, where it has been made for centuries. Traditionally boiled in brine with mahaleb and mastic, it has a distinctive flavor used in many Levantine sweets.
recipes.description: Traditional Palestinian white cheese from Nablus, boiled with mahaleb spice and essential for kunafa and Middle Eastern pastries.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 90°F.
Add starter culture, stir, and ripen for 15 minutes.
Add diluted rennet, stir gently. Let set 45-60 minutes until firm curd.
Cut curd into 1/2-inch cubes. Let rest 10 minutes.
Stir gently for 20 minutes at 90°F.
Drain whey and transfer curds to rectangular molds.
Press at 10 lbs for 4-6 hours.
Cut pressed cheese into 3x4 inch rectangular pieces.
Make spiced brine: dissolve salt in water, add mahaleb and mastic, bring to boil.
Boil cheese pieces in spiced brine for 5-10 minutes until they float.
Let cool in brine and store refrigerated.
For desserts, soak in fresh water overnight to remove excess salt.

notes: The boiling step in spiced brine is unique to Nabulsi cheese
Mahaleb (ground cherry pits) gives the distinctive slightly bitter-almond flavor
Mastic adds a subtle pine/resin note
Must be desalted before use in kunafa and other sweets

recipes.title: Traditional Jibneh Arabieh (Arabian White Cheese)
recipes.source_note: Jibneh Arabieh ('Arabian cheese') is the generic term for traditional white brine cheeses made throughout the Arabian Peninsula. Simple and mild, it's been a staple food for Bedouin and settled communities alike.
recipes.description: Simple Arabian white cheese, mild and versatile - a staple food throughout the Arabian Peninsula for millennia.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 90°F.
Add diluted rennet (no starter needed for this simple cheese), stir gently.
Let set 45-60 minutes until firm curd.
Cut curd into 1-inch cubes. Let rest 10 minutes.
Gently ladle curds into a cloth-lined colander.
If adding nigella seeds, fold them into curds now.
Tie cloth and hang to drain for 6-8 hours.
Cut drained cheese into blocks.
Make brine (about 8% salt solution) and submerge cheese.
Store in brine, refrigerated. Ready to eat after 1 week.

notes: This is one of the simplest traditional cheeses - rennet only, no starter
Nigella seeds (habbat al-barakah/black seed) are a popular addition
Traditionally made from whatever milk was available: goat, sheep, cow, or camel
Mild flavor, perfect with flatbread, olives, and Middle Eastern breakfast

recipes.title: Traditional Piave (Veneto)
recipes.source_note: Piave cheese is named after the Piave River in the Dolomite mountains of Veneto. While the formalized version dates to the 1960s, similar cheeses have been made in the Belluno province for centuries.
recipes.description: Alpine cheese from the Dolomites with a sweet, nutty flavor that intensifies with age - Italy's answer to Parmesan for grating.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 95°F. Add calcium chloride if using pasteurized milk.
Add starter culture, stir well, and ripen for 30 minutes.
Add diluted rennet, stir gently. Let set 30-35 minutes until clean break.
Cut curd into 1/4-inch cubes (small). Let rest 5 minutes.
Slowly raise temperature to 118°F over 30 minutes while stirring.
Continue stirring at 118°F for 30 minutes until curds are firm.
Drain whey and transfer curds to mold.
Press at 20 lbs for 30 minutes. Flip and press at 40 lbs for 12 hours.
Brine for 24-48 hours in saturated salt solution.
Age at 55°F and 85% humidity. Fresco: 1 month; Mezzano: 6 months; Vecchio: 12 months; Stravecchio: 18+ months.

notes: Piave becomes increasingly hard and intense with age
Young Piave (Fresco) is mild and sliceable; aged (Vecchio) is hard and grateable
The flavor develops sweet, butterscotch notes with proper aging

recipes.title: Traditional Montasio (Friuli-Venezia Giulia)
recipes.source_note: Montasio was created by Benedictine monks at Moggio Udinese Abbey in the 1200s. Named after the Montasio mountain massif, it's a cornerstone of Friulian cuisine and essential for frico (crispy cheese wafers).
recipes.description: Medieval Alpine cheese from the Julian Alps, essential for making frico - the crispy cheese wafers of Friuli.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 93°F. Add calcium chloride if using pasteurized milk.
Add starter culture, stir well, and ripen for 20 minutes.
Add diluted rennet, stir gently. Let set 25-30 minutes until clean break.
Cut curd into rice-sized grains. Let rest 5 minutes.
Slowly raise temperature to 115°F over 30 minutes while stirring constantly.
Continue stirring at 115°F for 20 minutes until curds are firm.
Drain whey and transfer curds to mold.
Press at 15 lbs for 30 minutes. Flip and press at 35 lbs for 12 hours.
Brine for 24-36 hours in saturated salt solution.
Age at 50-55°F and 85% humidity. Fresco: 2 months; Mezzano: 5-10 months; Stravecchio: 12-18 months.

notes: Young Montasio is semi-soft with mild, milky flavor
Aged Montasio becomes hard, sharp, and excellent for grating
Essential for frico - shredded cheese cooked into crispy wafers

recipes.title: Traditional Bra (Piedmont)
recipes.source_note: Bra cheese is named after the town of Bra in Cuneo province, Piedmont, where it has been made and traded since medieval times. There are two types: Tenero (soft) and Duro (hard).
recipes.description: Piedmontese cheese from the town of Bra, made in two styles - soft Tenero for eating and hard Duro for grating.

instructions.text: Combine milks and heat to 90°F. Add calcium chloride if using pasteurized.
Add starter culture, stir well, and ripen for 30 minutes.
Add diluted rennet, stir gently. Let set 40-50 minutes until clean break.
Cut curd into 1/2-inch cubes. Let rest 10 minutes.
Stir gently for 20 minutes while maintaining 90°F.
For Bra Tenero: Keep curds softer, minimal heating. For Bra Duro: Raise to 104°F.
Drain whey and transfer curds to molds.
Press at 15 lbs for 2 hours. Flip and press at 30 lbs for 12 hours.
Dry salt or brine for 12-24 hours.
Age at 55°F. Bra Tenero: 45 days minimum. Bra Duro: 6+ months.

recipes.temperature: 90°F for Tenero, up to 104°F for Duro, 55°F aging
notes: Bra Tenero has a soft, elastic paste and mild flavor
Bra Duro is hard, grainy, and sharp - suitable for grating
Traditional Bra often includes small amounts of sheep or goat milk
Bra d'Alpeggio is made only in summer from high pasture milk

recipes.title: Traditional Toma Piemontese
recipes.source_note: Toma is a generic name for traditional Alpine cheeses made throughout Piedmont and the Aosta Valley for centuries. Each valley has its own variation, but all share the characteristic semi-soft texture and earthy flavor.
recipes.description: Traditional Piedmontese Alpine cheese, varying by valley but always earthy and semi-soft - the everyday cheese of mountain communities.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 95°F. Add calcium chloride if using pasteurized milk.
Add starter culture, stir well, and ripen for 30 minutes.
Add diluted rennet, stir gently. Let set 35-45 minutes until clean break.
Cut curd into 1/2-inch cubes. Let rest 5 minutes.
Stir gently while raising temperature to 104°F over 20 minutes.
Continue stirring at 104°F for 15 minutes.
Drain whey and transfer curds to flat round molds.
Press lightly at 10 lbs for 2 hours.
Flip and press at 20 lbs for 8-12 hours.
Dry salt or brine for 12 hours.
Age at 50-55°F and 90% humidity for 15-60 days, turning regularly.

notes: Toma is a family of cheeses - each valley makes its own version
Semi-soft texture with natural gray-brown rind
Younger Toma is mild and milky; older becomes more complex
Toma Piemontese has DOP status; many local tomas do not

recipes.title: Traditional Puzzone di Moena (Spretz Tzaorì)
recipes.source_note: Puzzone di Moena (also called Spretz Tzaorì in Ladin) translates as 'stinky one from Moena.' This pungent washed-rind cheese has been made in the Fassa Valley of Trentino since medieval times.
recipes.description: Pungent Trentino cheese whose name means 'stinky one' - a traditional washed-rind Alpine cheese with intense aroma and flavor.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 95°F.
Add starter and B. linens, stir well, and ripen for 30 minutes.
Add diluted rennet, stir gently. Let set 35-40 minutes until clean break.
Cut curd into 1/2-inch cubes. Let rest 10 minutes.
Raise temperature to 104°F over 20 minutes while stirring.
Continue stirring for 20 minutes at 104°F.
Drain whey and transfer curds to round molds.
Press at 15 lbs for 2 hours. Flip and press at 30 lbs for 12 hours.
Dry salt all surfaces. Let rest 24 hours.
Age at 55°F and 95% humidity, washing with brine 2-3 times per week.
Age for 3-6 months. The rind should become sticky and orange-brown.

notes: The name 'Puzzone' (stinky) is well-earned - this is a very pungent cheese
The aroma is much stronger than the flavor, which is rich and savory
Traditional aging was in caves of the Dolomites
DOP protected as part of the Trentino cheese tradition

recipes.title: Traditional Canestrato (Sicilian Basket Cheese)
recipes.source_note: Canestrato gets its name from 'canestro' (basket) - the woven reed baskets traditionally used to drain and shape the cheese, which leave distinctive marks on the rind. It's been made in Sicily since ancient Greek and Roman times.
recipes.description: Ancient Sicilian cheese marked by its basket mold, made from sheep's milk with a sharp, tangy flavor that intensifies with age.

instructions.text: Heat sheep's milk to 95°F.
Add starter culture, stir well, and ripen for 20 minutes.
Add diluted rennet, stir gently. Let set 30-40 minutes until firm curd.
Cut curd into 1/4-inch cubes. Let rest 5 minutes.
Raise temperature to 118°F over 30 minutes while stirring.
Continue stirring for 20 minutes at 118°F until curds are firm.
Drain whey. If making Pepato, fold in peppercorns now.
Transfer curds to basket-weave molds (or regular molds with textured liner).
Press at 20 lbs for 2 hours. Flip and press at 40 lbs for 12 hours.
Dry salt all surfaces over 3-4 days.
Age at 55°F and 85% humidity for 4-12 months.

notes: The basket-weave pattern on the rind is the signature of canestrato
Canestrato Siciliano DOP must be made from sheep's milk
Canestrato Pepato has whole black peppercorns folded in
Young canestrato is semi-hard and tangy; aged becomes hard and sharp

recipes.title: Traditional Castelmagno (Piedmont)
recipes.source_note: Castelmagno is one of Italy's most ancient and prestigious cheeses, first documented in 1277 when it was accepted as payment of debts. Made in only three communes in the Grana Valley, it develops natural blue veining with age.
recipes.description: Ancient Piedmontese cheese that develops natural blue veining - one of Italy's rarest and most prestigious cheeses since the 13th century.

instructions.text: Combine milks and heat to 95°F.
Add starter culture, stir well, and ripen for 30 minutes.
Add diluted rennet, stir gently. Let set 45-60 minutes.
Cut curd into 1/2-inch cubes. Let rest 15 minutes.
Stir gently for 20 minutes at 95°F.
Drain whey. Let curds rest for 24-48 hours at room temperature, developing natural acid.
Break up the matted curd and mix with fresh curds from a new batch (traditional method).
Salt the mixed curds and transfer to molds.
Press at 20 lbs for 2 hours. Flip and press at 35 lbs for 24 hours.
Age at 50°F and 95% humidity for 2-6 months.
Blue veining develops naturally in cracks and crevices without inoculation.

notes: Traditional Castelmagno uses curds from two consecutive days mixed together
The natural blue veining comes from wild Penicillium in the aging caves
Young Castelmagno is ivory and crumbly; aged develops blue-green veins
One of Italy's rarest DOP cheeses, made in only 3 communes

recipes.title: Traditional Robiola (Piedmont)
recipes.source_note: Robiola is one of Italy's most ancient cheeses, possibly dating to Celtic times. The name may derive from the town of Robbio or from 'rubeolus' (reddish) describing the rind. Made in various forms throughout Piedmont and Lombardy.
recipes.description: Ancient soft Italian cheese from the hills of Piedmont and Lombardy, creamy and mild with a thin edible rind.

instructions.text: Combine milks and heat to 86°F.
Add starter culture, stir, and ripen for 30 minutes.
Add diluted rennet (very small amount), stir gently. Let set 12-18 hours at room temperature.
The curd should be very soft and delicate.
Gently ladle the soft curd into small round molds.
Let drain at room temperature for 24 hours, flipping carefully several times.
Unmold and salt lightly.
Fresh Robiola can be eaten immediately.
For aged Robiola, place at 55°F and 85% humidity for 1-3 weeks.
A thin wrinkled rind will develop; the interior should remain creamy.

notes: Robiola is a family of cheeses with many regional variations
Robiola di Roccaverano DOP uses goat or mixed milk
Fresh Robiola is very mild and creamy; aged develops more tang
The thin, wrinkled rind is edible and adds character

recipes.title: Traditional Queijo da Serra (Portuguese Mountain Cheese)
recipes.source_note: Queijo da Serra da Estrela is Portugal's most famous cheese, made in the highest mountain range in continental Portugal since at least the 12th century. Uniquely, it uses thistle rennet instead of animal rennet.
recipes.description: Portugal's most prestigious cheese, made with thistle rennet and sheep's milk, with a rich, runny interior when perfectly ripe.

instructions.text: Prepare thistle rennet: Steep dried cardoon flowers in 1/2 cup warm water for 2-3 hours or overnight.
Strain the thistle infusion through fine cloth. This is your rennet.
Heat sheep's milk to 86-90°F.
Add thistle rennet (about 1/4 cup per gallon). Stir gently.
Let set for 1-2 hours until a soft curd forms (thistle rennet works slower than animal rennet).
Gently cut curd into large pieces and ladle into cloth-lined molds.
Let drain at room temperature for 24-48 hours, flipping several times.
Salt the surface and let dry for 24 hours.
Age at 50-55°F and 90% humidity for 30-45 days minimum.
When ripe, the rind should be firm but the interior should be soft and almost runny.

notes: Thistle (cardoon) rennet is essential for authentic Serra cheese and makes it vegetarian
When perfectly ripe, cut off the top and eat the creamy interior with a spoon
The texture should be semi-liquid ('amanteigado') when at room temperature
DOP protected; only cheese made in the Serra da Estrela region can use this name

recipes.title: Traditional São Jorge (Azorean)
recipes.source_note: São Jorge cheese has been made on the Azorean island of São Jorge since the 15th century, introduced by Flemish settlers. The volcanic island's pastures and oceanic climate create a unique terroir for this hard, sharp cheese.
recipes.description: Sharp, tangy cheese from the Azores, introduced by Flemish settlers and perfected over centuries of island tradition.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 90°F.
Add starter culture, stir well, and ripen for 45 minutes.
Add diluted rennet, stir gently. Let set 45-60 minutes until firm curd.
Cut curd into 1/2-inch cubes. Let rest 10 minutes.
Slowly raise temperature to 100°F over 30 minutes while stirring.
Continue stirring for 30 minutes at 100°F.
Drain whey and transfer curds to molds.
Press at 20 lbs for 2 hours. Flip and press at 40 lbs for 24 hours.
Brine for 24-48 hours or dry salt over several days.
Age at 55°F and 85% humidity for 3-7 months, turning weekly.

notes: The Azores' volcanic soil and humid climate give São Jorge its distinctive flavor
Young São Jorge (3 months) is semi-hard and tangy
Aged São Jorge (7+ months) is hard, sharp, and excellent for grating
DOP protected; only cheese made on São Jorge island can bear this name

recipes.title: Traditional Queso Chihuahua (Mexican Menonita)
recipes.source_note: Queso Chihuahua, also called Queso Menonita, was introduced by German-speaking Mennonite settlers who arrived in Chihuahua, Mexico in the 1920s. Their Dutch/German cheesemaking traditions adapted to Mexican tastes.
recipes.description: Mild, buttery Mexican cheese introduced by Mennonite settlers, now essential for queso fundido and Mexican cuisine.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 86°F. Add calcium chloride if using pasteurized milk.
Add starter culture, stir well, and ripen for 30 minutes.
Add diluted rennet, stir gently. Let set 30-40 minutes until clean break.
Cut curd into 1/2-inch cubes. Let rest 5 minutes.
Slowly raise temperature to 102°F over 30 minutes while stirring.
Remove about 1/3 of whey. Replace with warm water to wash curds (this creates the mild flavor).
Continue stirring for 20 minutes at 102°F.
Drain whey and add salt to curds.
Transfer to molds. Press at 15 lbs for 30 minutes. Flip and press at 30 lbs for 8-12 hours.
Air dry for 1-2 days, then wax or vacuum seal.
Age at 55°F for 2-4 weeks.

notes: The curd washing creates the characteristic mild, buttery flavor
Excellent melting cheese for queso fundido and quesadillas
Similar to Gouda in technique due to Mennonite origins
Also sold as 'Queso Menonita' or just 'Chihuahua'

recipes.title: Traditional Queso Oaxaca (String Cheese)
recipes.source_note: Queso Oaxaca is a pasta filata cheese developed in Oaxaca, Mexico, combining indigenous cheesemaking traditions with Spanish techniques. It's traditionally formed into long ropes wound into balls.
recipes.description: Mexican string cheese formed into distinctive balls of wound ribbons, essential for quesadillas and melting over Mexican dishes.

instructions.text: Add citric acid solution to cold milk, stir well. Heat to 90°F.
Remove from heat, add diluted rennet, stir gently. Let set 15-20 minutes until clean break.
Cut curd into 1-inch cubes. Let rest 5 minutes.
Slowly heat to 105°F while stirring gently.
Drain curds and let mat at 100°F for 1-2 hours until pH reaches 5.2-5.3.
Cut matted curd into strips. Heat water to 170°F with salt.
Stretch curd in hot water until smooth and elastic.
Pull the stretched curd into long ribbons about 1/2 inch wide.
Wind the ribbons into a ball, tucking the end underneath.
Cool in ice water for 15 minutes to set shape.
Store in light brine or eat fresh within 1 week.

notes: The distinctive ball of wound ribbons is traditional to Oaxaca
Pull apart the ribbons ('strings') for eating or melting
Similar to mozzarella in technique but formed differently
Essential for authentic quesadillas and tlayudas

recipes.title: Traditional Cotija (Mexican Aged Cheese)
recipes.source_note: Cotija is named after the town of Cotija de la Paz in Michoacán. While Mexican cheesemaking evolved after Spanish contact, Cotija developed into a distinctly Mexican aged cheese, essential for finishing tacos, elotes, and many Mexican dishes.
recipes.description: Salty, crumbly Mexican aged cheese named for a Michoacán town - the 'Mexican Parmesan' essential for finishing dishes.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 90°F.
Add starter culture, stir well, and ripen for 45 minutes.
Add diluted rennet, stir gently. Let set 45-60 minutes until firm curd.
Cut curd into 1/2-inch cubes. Let rest 10 minutes.
Raise temperature to 100°F over 20 minutes while stirring.
Continue stirring for 30 minutes at 100°F until curds are firm.
Drain whey. Add salt (more than most cheeses - Cotija is salty).
Transfer to cylindrical molds. Press at 20 lbs for 2 hours.
Flip and press at 40 lbs for 24 hours.
Air dry for 3-5 days until surface is dry.
Age at 55°F and 80% humidity for 3-12 months. Turn weekly.

notes: Cotija is saltier than most cheeses - this aids preservation in hot climates
Young Cotija (3 months) is crumbly like feta
Aged Cotija (añejo, 12+ months) is hard and grateable like Parmesan
Essential for elotes (Mexican street corn), enchiladas, and tacos

recipes.title: Traditional Queso de Mano (Venezuelan)
recipes.source_note: Queso de Mano ('hand cheese') has been made in the Venezuelan llanos (plains) since colonial times. Named for the hand-kneading process that gives it its smooth, elastic texture, it's essential for Venezuelan cuisine.
recipes.description: Venezuelan stretched-curd cheese kneaded by hand, with a smooth, elastic texture essential for arepas and cachapas.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 90°F.
Add starter culture, stir, and ripen for 20 minutes.
Add diluted rennet, stir gently. Let set 30-40 minutes until clean break.
Cut curd into 1-inch cubes. Let rest 10 minutes.
Slowly raise temperature to 100°F while stirring.
Drain curds and let mat at warm room temperature for 2-3 hours.
Test for stretch in hot water (170°F). When ready, curds will stretch smoothly.
Knead the curd by hand (hence 'de mano') in hot water until smooth and elastic.
Work in salt while kneading.
Form into flat rounds or balls.
Store in light brine or use fresh within 1 week.

notes: The hand-kneading gives Queso de Mano its characteristic smooth texture
Similar to mozzarella but with a firmer, denser texture
Essential for Venezuelan arepas and cachapas (corn pancakes)
Best eaten fresh when still warm and stretchy

recipes.title: Traditional Cuajada (Latin American Fresh Curd)
recipes.source_note: Cuajada (from 'cuajar,' to curdle) is one of the simplest and most ancient fresh cheeses, made throughout Latin America and Spain. It's essentially fresh curds, eaten immediately with honey or sugar.
recipes.description: Simple Latin American fresh curd cheese, often eaten as dessert with honey - the most basic form of cheese, enjoyed for millennia.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 95°F (barely warm).
Add diluted rennet and stir gently for 30 seconds.
Let sit undisturbed for 30-45 minutes until set like a soft junket.
The curd should be very soft and delicate, barely holding its shape.
Carefully spoon the soft curd into serving bowls.
Drizzle with honey, sprinkle with cinnamon, or add sugar to taste.
Serve immediately while still warm.

notes: Cuajada is meant to be eaten immediately - it's not a cheese to store
The texture should be like a soft custard or junket
Traditional Spanish cuajada uses sheep's milk
In Latin America, often eaten as a simple breakfast or dessert
This is cheese in its most elemental form

recipes.title: Traditional Requesón (Latin American Ricotta)
recipes.source_note: Requesón is the Spanish and Latin American equivalent of ricotta, made from the whey left over from other cheesemaking. The name means 're-curdled,' similar to ricotta meaning 're-cooked.'
recipes.description: Latin American whey cheese, the Spanish cousin of ricotta - light, fresh, and essential for both sweet and savory dishes.

instructions.text: Use fresh whey from cheese making (rennet-set whey works best).
Add milk if using. Heat slowly over medium heat.
As temperature approaches 185-195°F, white curds will begin to rise.
If curds don't form, add lemon juice one tablespoon at a time.
When curds are floating on top, remove from heat. Let rest 10 minutes.
Gently skim the curds with a slotted spoon into a fine strainer.
Let drain for 15-30 minutes.
Add salt if desired. Use immediately or refrigerate up to 5 days.

notes: The fresher the whey, the better the requesón
Acid-set cheese whey doesn't work as well as rennet-set whey
Used in Mexican enchiladas, with honey as dessert, or in pastries
Very light and low in fat since most fat stays in the original cheese

recipes.title: Traditional Bryndza (Carpathian Sheep Cheese)
recipes.source_note: Bryndza has been made by Vlach shepherds in the Carpathian Mountains for over a thousand years. It's the national cheese of Slovakia and essential to Polish and Slovak cuisine. Made from sheep's milk, it has a distinctively tangy, sharp flavor.
recipes.description: Ancient Carpathian sheep cheese with a sharp, tangy flavor - the national cheese of Slovakia and foundation of bryndzové halušky.

instructions.text: Heat sheep's milk to 90°F.
Add starter or allow to naturally sour for 1 hour.
Add diluted rennet, stir gently. Let set 45-60 minutes.
Cut curd into 1/2-inch cubes. Let rest 10 minutes.
Drain whey and hang curds in cloth to drain for 24 hours.
The drained curd (called 'hrudka' or 'žinčica base') should be crumbly.
Let the drained curd ripen at cool room temperature (55-60°F) for 1-2 weeks, breaking up and re-forming daily.
When properly ripened, the curd will be tangy and slightly sour.
Grind or mash the ripened curd until smooth and spreadable.
Mix in salt to taste.
Pack into containers. Refrigerate and use within 2-3 weeks.

notes: Authentic bryndza must be made from sheep's milk (at least 50% by EU regulations)
The ripening process develops the characteristic sharp, tangy flavor
Essential for bryndzové halušky (Slovak national dish) and pierogi fillings

recipes.title: Traditional Oscypek (Polish Smoked Sheep Cheese)
recipes.source_note: Oscypek has been made by Górale (Polish highlanders) in the Tatra Mountains since at least the 15th century, likely brought by Vlach shepherds. The distinctive spindle shape and decorative patterns are carved by hand into wooden molds.
recipes.description: Decorative smoked sheep cheese from the Polish Tatras, hand-carved into traditional spindle shapes by highland shepherds.

instructions.text: Combine milks and heat to 95°F.
Add diluted rennet, stir gently. Let set 30-40 minutes.
Cut curd finely into rice-sized grains.
Gather curds in cloth and squeeze out whey.
While still warm and pliable, knead the curd mass by hand.
Form into a spindle/lens shape (traditional oscypek form).
Press into decorative carved wooden molds to imprint traditional patterns.
Soak in saturated brine for 12-24 hours.
Air dry for 1-2 days.
Cold smoke over pine, spruce, or juniper wood for 1-2 weeks.
The finished cheese should be golden-brown with a smoky aroma.

notes: The decorative patterns are unique to each shepherd's molds
Authentic oscypek must be made in the Tatra region from specific sheep breeds
Often grilled and served with cranberry jam

recipes.title: Traditional Olomoucké Tvarůžky (Czech Stinky Cheese)
recipes.source_note: Olomoucké tvarůžky have been made in the Haná region of Moravia since at least the 15th century. One of the world's smelliest cheeses, it's made from soured quark and is virtually fat-free.
recipes.description: Intensely pungent Moravian cheese made from soured quark - one of the world's smelliest cheeses, fat-free and centuries old.

instructions.text: Start with very well-drained, low-fat quark or farmer's cheese.
Let the quark sour at room temperature for 2-3 days until it develops a sharp smell.
Knead the soured quark with salt (and caraway if using) until smooth.
Form into small disc shapes about 1 inch thick and 2 inches across.
Place on a rack in a ripening container with high humidity.
Ripen at 55-60°F and 90%+ humidity for 1-6 weeks.
Turn daily. A golden-yellow surface bacteria will develop (Brevibacterium linens).
The cheese is ready when golden-yellow throughout with an intense aroma.
Young tvarůžky (1-2 weeks) are milder; aged (6+ weeks) are extremely pungent.

notes: This is one of the world's smelliest cheeses - the aroma is INTENSE
Despite the smell, the flavor is savory, complex, and addictive
Traditionally served with bread, onions, and Czech beer
PGI protected; the only Czech cheese with EU protection

recipes.title: Traditional Telemea (Romanian White Cheese)
recipes.source_note: Telemea is Romania's most widespread traditional cheese, similar to feta but with regional variations. It may date back to the ancient Dacians. Made from sheep, goat, cow, or buffalo milk depending on the region.
recipes.description: Romania's essential white brine cheese, possibly dating to ancient Dacian times - the foundation of Romanian cuisine.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 90°F.
Add starter culture and ripen for 30 minutes.
Add diluted rennet, stir gently. Let set 45-60 minutes.
Cut curd into 1/2-inch cubes. Let rest 10 minutes.
Stir gently for 15 minutes at 90°F.
Let curds settle, drain most whey.
Transfer curds to a cloth-lined mold. Press lightly for 4-6 hours.
Cut the pressed cheese into 3-4 inch blocks.
Make brine (8-10% salt solution) and submerge cheese blocks.
Store in brine at refrigerator temperature for 2-4 weeks minimum.
Telemea can be stored in brine for many months.

notes: Telemea de Sibiu (sheep milk) and Telemea de Ibănești are PGI protected
The type of milk dramatically affects the flavor - sheep is richest
Essential for Romanian salads, mamaliga, and countless traditional dishes
Similar to feta but often softer and less tangy

recipes.title: Traditional Giuncata (Ancient Roman Rush Cheese)
recipes.source_note: Giuncata (from 'giunco' - rush/reed) is one of the oldest Italian cheeses, dating to ancient Rome. Described by Columella and other Roman writers, it was traditionally drained in rush baskets which gave it its name.
recipes.description: Ancient Roman fresh cheese drained in rush baskets, unchanged for over 2000 years - one of the oldest cheese recipes still made.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 95°F (no higher - this is a delicate cheese).
Add diluted rennet, stir very gently for 30 seconds.
Let set undisturbed for 30-45 minutes until a soft curd forms.
The curd should be soft and delicate, like a custard.
Very gently ladle the soft curd into rush baskets or fine-weave molds.
Let drain at room temperature for 2-4 hours. Do not press.
The finished cheese should be soft, moist, and delicate.
Eat immediately while fresh, with honey if desired.

notes: This cheese was described by Columella in 'De Re Rustica' (1st century AD)
The rush basket gives distinctive texture marks and the name 'giuncata'
Must be eaten within 1-2 days - it's not a cheese for keeping
Traditional Roman dessert when served with honey
Similar to modern junket but made with real milk and rennet

recipes.title: Traditional Pecorino Sardo (Sardinian)
recipes.source_note: Pecorino Sardo has been made in Sardinia since the Bronze Age, possibly 4000+ years. The island's unique sheep breeds and wild herbs create distinctive flavors. Two types exist: Dolce (young) and Maturo (aged).
recipes.description: Ancient Sardinian sheep cheese dating to the Bronze Age, made from milk of indigenous sheep grazing on wild Mediterranean herbs.

instructions.text: Heat sheep's milk to 95°F.
Add starter culture, stir well, and ripen for 20 minutes.
Add rennet, stir gently. Let set 30-40 minutes until firm curd.
Cut curd into 1/4-inch cubes (small). Let rest 5 minutes.
Slowly raise temperature to 113°F over 20 minutes while stirring.
Continue stirring for 15 minutes at 113°F.
Drain whey and transfer curds to molds.
Press at 20 lbs for 30 minutes. Flip and press at 40 lbs for 8-12 hours.
Dry salt or brine for 24-48 hours.
Age at 55°F and 85% humidity. Dolce: 1-2 months. Maturo: 4-8 months.

notes: Pecorino Sardo Dolce is soft, mild, and milky
Pecorino Sardo Maturo is hard, sharp, and excellent for grating
The wild herbs of Sardinian pastures (myrtle, wild fennel) flavor the milk
DOP protected; one of Italy's most ancient cheeses

recipes.title: Traditional Fiore Sardo (Smoked Sardinian Pecorino)
recipes.source_note: Fiore Sardo ('Sardinian Flower') is possibly the original Sardinian pecorino, predating even Pecorino Sardo. Made by shepherds in the mountainous interior and traditionally smoked over aromatic wood, it may date to the Nuragic civilization.
recipes.description: The original Sardinian cheese, smoked over aromatic wood by mountain shepherds - possibly 3000+ years old.

ingredients.prep_note: olive, myrtle, or local woods for smoking

instructions.text: Use fresh, still-warm sheep's milk (traditional) or heat to 95°F.
Add lamb rennet paste (no starter culture - this is a raw rennet-only cheese).
Let set 40-50 minutes until very firm curd.
Cut curd into small pieces and work by hand to expel whey.
Transfer to molds and press firmly by hand.
Let drain overnight at room temperature.
Brine or dry salt for 2-3 days.
Cold smoke over olive, myrtle, or local aromatic wood for 10-15 days.
Rub with olive oil periodically during aging.
Age at 50-55°F for 3-8 months minimum.

notes: Fiore Sardo uses NO starter culture - only lamb rennet paste
The smoking over aromatic Mediterranean woods is essential
The name 'Fiore' (flower) may refer to the flower-shaped molds once used
DOP protected; considered the original Sardinian cheese

recipes.title: Traditional Kefalotyri (Greek Hard Cheese)
recipes.source_note: Kefalotyri (meaning 'head cheese' from its shape) has been made in Greece since at least Byzantine times. It's the traditional hard cheese of Greece, used for grating and for making saganaki (pan-fried cheese).
recipes.description: Traditional Greek hard cheese for grating and frying, made since Byzantine times - the original cheese for saganaki.

instructions.text: Combine milks and heat to 95°F.
Add starter culture, stir well, and ripen for 30 minutes.
Add diluted rennet, stir gently. Let set 40-50 minutes until very firm.
Cut curd into 1/4-inch cubes. Let rest 10 minutes.
Raise temperature to 122°F over 40 minutes while stirring constantly.
Continue stirring at 122°F for 20 minutes until curds are very firm.
Drain whey and transfer curds to molds.
Press at 20 lbs for 1 hour. Flip and press at 50 lbs for 24 hours.
Brine for 24-48 hours in saturated salt solution.
Age at 55°F and 85% humidity for 3-12 months, turning weekly.

notes: Kefalotyri should be very hard - harder than most Italian pecorinos
The high cooking temperature creates the firm, dense texture
Essential for saganaki - fry thick slices in olive oil until golden
Young kefalotyri (3 months) for frying; aged (12+ months) for grating

recipes.title: Traditional Harzer Käse (Harz Mountain Cheese)
recipes.source_note: Harzer Käse originated in the Harz Mountains of central Germany, where it's been made since medieval times. Like Handkäse, it's a sour milk cheese but ripened with yellow surface mold to develop its characteristic sharp flavor.
recipes.description: Pungent German sour milk cheese from the Harz Mountains, ripened with yellow mold for a sharp, tangy flavor.

instructions.text: Use very low-fat quark, well-drained.
Let sour at room temperature for 24-48 hours.
Mix with salt and caraway seeds.
Form into small round or roll shapes.
Let dry at room temperature for 24 hours.
Place in ripening environment at 55-60°F and 90% humidity.
Turn daily. Yellow surface mold (Brevibacterium linens) will develop.
Ripen for 1-2 weeks until fully covered with golden-yellow rind.
The interior should remain white while the surface becomes golden and aromatic.

notes: Harzer is one of Germany's most protein-rich foods - virtually fat-free
The yellow surface bacteria create the characteristic sharp aroma
Popular among athletes and dieters for its high protein, low fat content
The longer it ripens, the more pungent it becomes

recipes.title: Traditional Rubing (Yunnan Goat Cheese)
recipes.source_note: Rubing ('milk cake') is a traditional cheese of the Bai and other ethnic minorities of Yunnan Province, China. It's one of the few traditional Chinese cheeses and has been made for centuries, typically from goat's milk.
recipes.description: Rare traditional Chinese cheese from Yunnan, made by the Bai people - firm and mild, typically grilled or fried.

ingredients.prep_note: traditionally from previous batch, or vinegar/lemon juice

instructions.text: Heat goat's milk to a rolling boil in a large pot.
Reduce heat to maintain a simmer.
Slowly add the sour liquid (traditional method uses whey from previous batch).
Stir gently as curds form and separate from the whey.
Continue simmering until curds are well-formed.
Drain curds through a cloth-lined strainer.
While still warm and pliable, press curds firmly into a block or round shape.
Weight down and press for 1-2 hours until firm.
Cut into squares or rectangles for cooking.
Store refrigerated; eat within 1 week.

notes: Rubing is unusual - it's one of the few traditional Chinese cheeses
Typically pan-fried, grilled, or stir-fried rather than eaten raw
The texture is firm and doesn't melt, similar to paneer or halloumi
Often served with salt and chili, or in stir-fries

recipes.title: Traditional Byaslag (Mongolian Fresh Cheese)
recipes.source_note: Byaslag is the Mongolian fresh cheese, softer than the dried aaruul. Made in every ger (yurt) when milk is abundant, it's eaten fresh or used in cooking. The simplest form is pressed between two boards.
recipes.description: Fresh Mongolian cheese pressed between boards in the ger - simpler than aaruul, eaten fresh when milk is plentiful.

instructions.text: Heat milk until just simmering.
Add kefir or yogurt and stir gently.
Continue heating gently until curds form and separate.
Drain curds through cloth.
Add salt if using.
Traditional method: Place curds in cloth between two flat boards.
Weight down the top board and press for 2-4 hours.
Remove from press and cut into slices.
Eat fresh or use in Mongolian dishes.

notes: Byaslag is softer and fresher than dried aaruul
The board-pressing technique is simple and traditional to the ger
Can be made from any available milk
Used in Mongolian dumplings (buuz) and noodle soups

recipes.title: Traditional Pecorino Toscano (Tuscan)
recipes.source_note: Pecorino Toscano has been made in Tuscany since at least Etruscan times, over 2500 years ago. Milder than Pecorino Romano, it's aged for less time and has a softer, more delicate flavor that complements Tuscan cuisine.
recipes.description: Ancient Tuscan sheep cheese dating to the Etruscans, milder and softer than Roman pecorino - the table cheese of Tuscany.

instructions.text: Heat sheep's milk to 95°F.
Add starter culture, stir, and ripen for 20 minutes.
Add diluted rennet, stir gently. Let set 25-35 minutes until clean break.
Cut curd into 1/2-inch cubes (larger than Romano). Let rest 10 minutes.
Slowly raise temperature to 108°F over 20 minutes while stirring.
Drain whey and transfer curds to molds.
Press at 15 lbs for 30 minutes. Flip and press at 30 lbs for 6-8 hours.
Dry salt or brine for 12-24 hours.
Age at 55°F and 85% humidity. Fresco: 20 days. Stagionato: 4+ months.

notes: Pecorino Toscano is milder and less salty than Pecorino Romano
Fresco (young) is soft and mild, perfect as table cheese
Stagionato (aged) is firmer with more complex flavor
DOP protected; essential to Tuscan cuisine

recipes.title: Traditional Pecorino Romano (Ancient Roman)
recipes.source_note: Pecorino Romano was part of the daily ration for Roman legions over 2000 years ago. Made in the countryside around Rome (now mostly in Sardinia), it's a hard, salty sheep cheese essential for pasta dishes like cacio e pepe.
recipes.description: The cheese of Roman legions, sharp and salty - essential for cacio e pepe and carbonara, unchanged for over 2000 years.

ingredients.prep_note: Romano is saltier than other pecorinos

instructions.text: Heat sheep's milk to 100°F (higher than Toscano).
Add starter, stir, and ripen for 15 minutes.
Add lamb rennet paste (traditional) or liquid rennet. Let set 20-25 minutes.
Cut curd into rice-sized grains (very small). Let rest 5 minutes.
Raise temperature to 118°F over 30 minutes while stirring constantly.
Continue stirring at 118°F for 20 minutes until curds are very firm.
Drain whey and transfer to molds. Press immediately.
Press at 25 lbs for 1 hour. Flip and press at 50 lbs for 24 hours.
Dry salt heavily over 2-3 weeks, or brine for several days.
Age at 55°F and 85% humidity for 5-8 months minimum.

notes: Pecorino Romano is saltier and sharper than other pecorinos
The small curd cut and high cooking temperature create the hard texture
Originally from Lazio, now mostly made in Sardinia
Essential for authentic cacio e pepe, carbonara, and amatriciana

recipes.title: Sakura Cream Cheese
recipes.description: Japanese-style fresh cream cheese infused with cherry blossom essence.

ingredients.item: acid (lemon juice, vinegar, or citric acid)

instructions.text: Heat whole cow's milk to 185-195°F (85-90°C), stirring occasionally to prevent scorching.
Remove from heat. Add acid slowly while stirring gently.
Curds will form immediately. Let rest 10 minutes.
Line colander with butter muslin. Ladle curds into colander.
Drain for 15-60 minutes depending on desired moisture.
Add salt and mix gently. Use immediately or refrigerate up to 1 week.

notes: High temperature (185-195°F) essential for acid coagulation
Add cherry blossom extract during mixing

missing_inputs: 1/4 cup acid (lemon juice, vinegar, or citric acid)

recipes.title: Japanese Camembert-Style
recipes.description: Japanese interpretation of Camembert with subtle umami notes.

instructions.text: Heat whole cow's milk to 90°F (32°C) in a water bath.
Add calcium chloride if using pasteurized milk. Sprinkle Flora Danica culture, P. camemberti, and Geotrichum over surface, let rehydrate 2 minutes, then stir in.
Ripen for 60-90 minutes. Add diluted rennet, stir gently for 30 seconds.
Let set 60-90 minutes until clean break. Cut curd into 1-inch cubes.
LADLE MOLDING: Gently ladle curds into molds - do not press or break up curds.
Drain at room temperature for 24-36 hours, flipping every 2-4 hours. Cheese will compress naturally.
Unmold and salt all surfaces lightly.
Age at 50-55°F (10-13°C), 90-95% humidity. Place on ripening mat.
White mold appears in 10-14 days. Flip daily until fully coated.
Wrap in cheese paper when fully coated. Continue aging until soft throughout.

notes: High humidity (90-95%) essential for P. camemberti growth
Ripe when center is soft and slightly bulging
Japanese cheesemakers adapted French techniques post-WWII

recipes.title: Hokkaido Gouda
recipes.description: Japanese Gouda-style cheese from Hokkaido dairy farms with rich, creamy flavor.

instructions.text: Heat whole cow's milk to 90°F (32°C) in a water bath.
Add calcium chloride if using pasteurized milk. Sprinkle MM100 culture over surface, let rehydrate 2 minutes, then stir in.
Ripen for 15 minutes. Add diluted rennet, stir gently for 30 seconds.
Let set 45 minutes until clean break. Cut curd into 3/8-inch cubes.
CURD WASHING: Remove 1/3 of whey. Replace with 140°F (60°C) water to reduce acidity and create sweet flavor.
Raise temperature to 100°F (38°C) over 30 minutes while stirring.
Continue stirring at 100°F for 30 minutes until curds are firm.
Drain whey. Transfer curds to mold.
Press at 20 lbs for 30 min, then 40 lbs for 2 hours, then 50 lbs for 12 hours. Flip during pressing.
Brine in saturated salt solution for 8-12 hours.
Air dry until surface is no longer tacky. Wax if desired. Age at 55°F, 85% humidity.

notes: Curd washing removes lactose, creating sweet flavor
MM100 culture with Leuconostoc creates small eyes
Hokkaido has ideal climate for dairy farming

recipes.title: Korean String Cheese
recipes.description: Korean-style mozzarella string cheese, popular as snack and banchan.

instructions.text: Heat whole cow's milk to 95°F (35°C) in a water bath for stable temperature.
Add calcium chloride if using pasteurized milk. Sprinkle thermophilic culture over surface, let rehydrate 2 minutes, then stir in.
Add diluted rennet, stir gently for 30 seconds. Let set 45-60 minutes until clean break.
Cut curd into 1/2-inch cubes. Let rest 5 minutes.
Slowly raise temperature to 105°F (41°C) over 30 minutes, stirring gently.
Drain whey. Let curds mat and acidify at 85-90°F until pH reaches 5.2-5.4 (typically 2-4 hours).
STRETCHING: Heat water to 170-180°F (77-82°C). Cut curds into strips, submerge in hot water.
Knead and stretch curds until smooth, shiny, and elastic. Work quickly while curd is hot.
Add salt during stretching. Form into desired shape (ball, braid, log).
Place in ice water bath to set shape. Store in brine or whey.
Same day

notes: Stretching in 170-180°F water is essential for pasta filata texture
pH must be 5.2-5.4 before stretching or curd won't stretch properly

recipes.title: Majdoule (Majdouleh)
recipes.description: Lebanese braided cheese similar to Syrian cheese ropes.

instructions.text: Heat whole cow's milk to 95°F (35°C) in a water bath for stable temperature.

Cut curd into 1/2-inch cubes. Let rest 5 minutes.
Slowly raise temperature to 105°F (41°C) over 30 minutes, stirring gently.

STRETCHING: Heat water to 170-180°F (77-82°C). Cut curds into strips, submerge in hot water.
Knead and stretch curds until smooth, shiny, and elastic. Work quickly while curd is hot.
Add salt during stretching. Form into desired shape (ball, braid, log).

Age at 50-55°F for Fresh or 1-2 weeks brined for flavor development.

notes: Stretching in 170-180°F water is essential for pasta filata texture
pH must be 5.2-5.4 before stretching or curd won't stretch properly

recipes.title: Aged Queso Chihuahua
recipes.description: Aged version of Chihuahua cheese with sharper, more complex flavor.

instructions.text: Heat whole cow's milk to 90°F (32°C) in a water bath.
Add calcium chloride if using pasteurized milk. Sprinkle MM100 culture over surface, let rehydrate 2 minutes, then stir in.
Ripen for 15 minutes. Add diluted rennet, stir gently for 30 seconds.
Let set 45 minutes until clean break. Cut curd into 3/8-inch cubes.
CURD WASHING: Remove 1/3 of whey. Replace with 140°F (60°C) water to reduce acidity and create sweet flavor.
Raise temperature to 100°F (38°C) over 30 minutes while stirring.
Continue stirring at 100°F for 30 minutes until curds are firm.
Drain whey. Transfer curds to mold.
Press at 20 lbs for 30 min, then 40 lbs for 2 hours, then 50 lbs for 12 hours. Flip during pressing.
Brine in saturated salt solution for 8-12 hours.
Air dry until surface is no longer tacky. Wax if desired. Age at 55°F, 85% humidity.

notes: Curd washing removes lactose, creating sweet flavor
MM100 culture with Leuconostoc creates small eyes

ingredients.item: thermophilic starter culture (TA061 with L. helveticus)

instructions.text: Heat whole cow's milk to 90°F (32°C).
Add calcium chloride if pasteurized. Add thermophilic culture with L. helveticus.
Ripen 30 min. Add diluted rennet. Let set 30-45 min until clean break.
Cut curd into rice-sized pieces (1/8 inch).
ALPINE COOKING: Gradually raise to 120-130°F (49-54°C) over 45 min, stirring constantly.
Continue stirring at cooking temp 30-45 min until curds firm and squeaky.
Gather curds under whey. Transfer to mold.
Press at 25 lbs 30 min, 50 lbs 2 hours, 75 lbs 12 hours.
Brine 24-48 hours depending on size.
Age at 55°F, 90-95% humidity. Rub with brine twice weekly.
