recipes.description: Historic pressed sheep's milk cheese from the Pyrenean Roncal Valley. Spain's first cheese to receive PDO status. Hard, dry texture with intense, piquant flavor and notes of herbs and nuts. Made only from Rasa and Latxa sheep.

instructions.text: Heat sheep's milk to 86°F (30°C). Add starter, ripen 30 minutes.
Add calcium chloride, then rennet. Let set 45 minutes until firm break.
Cut curds into very small 1/4-inch cubes.
Heat to 104°F (40°C) over 40 minutes while stirring constantly.
Continue stirring until curds are very firm and dry, about 40 minutes.
Drain and press heavily at 30 lbs for 2 hours, flip, then 50 lbs for 24 hours.
Brine in saturated solution for 48 hours.
Age at 50°F (10°C) and 80% humidity for minimum 4 months, up to 12 months.

notes: First Spanish cheese to receive Denominacion de Origen (1981)
Made only from December to July when sheep graze mountain pastures
Heavy pressing creates the characteristic dense, dry texture
Transhumance tradition - sheep move between mountain and valley pastures

recipes.title: Queso Zamorano (Castilian Sheep Cheese)
recipes.source_note: PDO sheep's milk cheese from Zamora province, Castilla y Leon.
recipes.description: Firm, flavorful sheep's milk cheese from Zamora in the Castilian plains. Made from Churra and Castellana sheep, it has a grainy, crumbly texture with intense, slightly spicy flavor. Often compared to Manchego but with its own distinct character.

instructions.text: Heat sheep's milk to 82°F (28°C). Add starter, ripen 45 minutes.
Add calcium chloride, then rennet. Let set 50-60 minutes.
Cut curds into small 1/4-inch cubes.
Heat to 102°F (39°C) over 35 minutes while stirring.
Continue stirring until curds are firm and dry, about 35 minutes.
Drain and press at 25 lbs for 2 hours, flip, then 45 lbs for 24 hours.
Brine 36 hours.
Age at 50-55°F (10-13°C) for minimum 3 months, up to 12 months.

notes: Churra sheep are famous for their milk's high fat and protein content
Zamora province has centuries of sheep cheese tradition
Similar to Manchego but made from different sheep breeds

recipes.title: San Simon da Costa (Galician Smoked Cow Cheese)
recipes.source_note: PDO smoked cow's milk cheese from Galicia with distinctive teardrop shape.
recipes.description: Distinctive teardrop-shaped smoked cheese from Galicia. Smoked over birch wood, it has a glossy amber exterior and creamy, buttery interior. The unique shape and smoking tradition date back centuries.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 86°F (30°C). Add starter, ripen 30 minutes.
Add calcium chloride, then rennet. Let set 40 minutes.
Cut curds into 1/2-inch cubes. Rest 5 minutes.
Heat to 98°F (37°C) over 25 minutes while stirring.
Drain and press into teardrop/pear-shaped molds at 20 lbs for 12 hours.
Brine 12 hours.
Age at 50°F (10°C) for 3-4 weeks, then cold smoke over birch wood for 2-3 weeks.
Continue aging 2-4 more weeks after smoking.

notes: Birch smoking is traditional - gives distinctive golden-brown rind
Galicia's humid climate makes smoking an effective preservation method
Interior stays creamy despite the firm smoked exterior

missing_inputs: as needed  birch wood chips for smoking

recipes.title: Afuega'l Pitu (Asturian Spicy Cheese)
recipes.source_note: PDO cheese from Asturias, name means 'fire in the throat'.
recipes.description: Ancient Asturian cheese whose name means 'fire in the throat' in Asturian dialect - a testament to its dense, paste-like texture that sticks to the palate. Made in two versions: white (natural) or roxu (with paprika). Conical or gourd-shaped.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 72°F (22°C) - barely warm. Add starter.
Add only 2 drops of rennet - this is primarily an acid-set cheese.
Let set at room temperature 24-48 hours until thick, acidic curd forms.
Hang curd in cheesecloth to drain for 24-48 hours.
Mix salt (and paprika for roxu version) into the drained curd.
Pack into conical (atroncau) or gourd-shaped (trapu) molds.
Age at 50°F (10°C) for 2-8 weeks.
Rind will develop natural molds - leave or brush as preferred.

notes: One of Spain's oldest cheese-making traditions
Afuega'l Pitu means 'chokes the chicken' - refers to dense, sticky texture
Roxu (red) version uses local paprika; blancu (white) is natural
Two traditional shapes: atroncau (cone) and trapu (gourd/pumpkin)

recipes.title: Garrotxa (Catalan Goat Cheese)
recipes.source_note: Revived Catalan goat cheese with distinctive gray mold rind.
recipes.description: Semi-firm Catalan goat cheese with a distinctive fuzzy gray Penicillium mold rind. Nearly extinct in the 1980s, it was revived by artisan cheesemakers. Mild, nutty goat flavor with earthy undertones from the natural rind.

instructions.text: Heat goat's milk to 86°F (30°C). Add starter and optional P. candidum, ripen 30 minutes.
Add calcium chloride, then rennet. Let set 45 minutes.
Cut curds into 1/2-inch cubes. Rest 5 minutes.
Heat to 95°F (35°C) over 20 minutes while stirring gently.
Stir until curds firm slightly, about 15 minutes.
Drain and press lightly at 10 lbs for 1 hour, flip, then 15 lbs for 6 hours.
Salt surfaces.
Age at 50-55°F (10-13°C) and 90% humidity for 3-8 weeks. Gray mold will develop naturally.

notes: Named for the Garrotxa region in Catalonia's Pyrenean foothills
Was nearly extinct until 1981 revival by artisan cheesemakers
Gray Penicillium mold rind is characteristic - don't brush it off
Milder than many goat cheeses due to the mold-ripening

recipes.title: Queso Majorero (Canarian Goat Cheese)
recipes.source_note: PDO goat cheese from Fuerteventura, Canary Islands.
recipes.description: Pressed goat cheese from Fuerteventura in the Canary Islands, made from the native Majorera goat. Can be fresh, semi-cured, or aged. Traditionally rubbed with paprika, oil, or roasted corn flour (gofio). Intense goat flavor with island terroir.

ingredients.item: paprika, olive oil, or gofio for rind (optional)

instructions.text: Heat goat's milk to 82°F (28°C). Add starter, ripen 30 minutes.
Add calcium chloride, then rennet. Let set 45 minutes.
Cut curds into 1/2-inch cubes. Rest 5 minutes.
Heat to 95°F (35°C) over 20 minutes while stirring.
Drain and press into traditional palm-leaf patterned molds at 20 lbs for 12-24 hours.
Brine 12-24 hours depending on size.
Optionally rub rind with paprika, olive oil, or gofio (roasted corn flour).
Age at 50-55°F (10-13°C): 1-2 weeks for fresh, 1-2 months semi-cured, 3-6 months for cured.

notes: Majorera goats are native to Fuerteventura, adapted to arid conditions
Palm leaf mold pattern on rind is traditional
Gofio coating is unique to Canarian cheese tradition

recipes.title: Queso Arzua-Ulloa (Galician Soft Cow Cheese)
recipes.source_note: PDO soft cow's milk cheese from inland Galicia.
recipes.description: Soft, creamy cow's milk cheese from the Arzua and Ulloa regions of Galicia. Buttery and mild with a thin, edible rind. One of Spain's most approachable cheeses, often eaten at breakfast or as a snack.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 86°F (30°C). Add starter, ripen 30 minutes.
Add calcium chloride, then rennet. Let set 50 minutes for soft curd.
Cut curds into 3/4-inch cubes. Rest 10 minutes.
Stir very gently for 15 minutes - do not heat further.
Ladle curds into molds without pressing.
Drain at room temperature 12-24 hours, flipping every 4-6 hours.
Salt surfaces lightly.
Age at 46-50°F (8-10°C) and 85-90% humidity for 2-4 weeks.

notes: One of Spain's mildest, most approachable cheeses
Galicia's green, humid climate is ideal for soft cheese
Often served with membrillo (quince paste) for dessert
Similar to Tetilla but flatter disc shape

recipes.title: Queso Iberico (Spanish Mixed Milk Cheese)
recipes.source_note: Classic Spanish blend of cow, sheep, and goat milks.
recipes.description: Traditional Spanish cheese blending cow, sheep, and goat milks in varying proportions. The combination creates a complex, balanced flavor - the creaminess of cow, richness of sheep, and tang of goat. A true taste of the Iberian Peninsula.

instructions.text: Combine all three milks. Heat to 86°F (30°C). Add starter, ripen 45 minutes.
Add calcium chloride, then rennet. Let set 45 minutes.
Cut curds into 1/2-inch cubes. Rest 5 minutes.
Heat to 100°F (38°C) over 30 minutes while stirring.
Continue stirring until curds firm, about 25 minutes.
Drain and press at 20 lbs for 2 hours, flip, then 35 lbs for 12 hours.
Brine 24 hours.
Age at 50-55°F (10-13°C) for 2-6 months.

notes: Milk ratios can vary - some versions favor sheep, others cow
Three-milk blend is traditional throughout central Spain
Each milk contributes different characteristics to the final cheese
The name 'Iberico' references the Iberian Peninsula

recipes.title: Taleggio Lombardo (Lombardy Washed Rind)
recipes.source_note: DOP washed-rind cheese from Lombardy's Val Taleggio.
recipes.description: Pungent, creamy washed-rind cheese from the valleys of Lombardy. The characteristic orange rind and strong aroma belie a mild, fruity interior that melts beautifully.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 90°F (32°C). Add starter and B. linens, ripen 30 minutes.
Add calcium chloride if using pasteurized milk. Add rennet and let set 45-60 minutes until soft curd forms.
Cut curds into 2-inch cubes. Let rest 10 minutes.
Gently ladle curds into square molds - do NOT press. Allow to drain naturally at room temperature.
Flip every 2-3 hours for 12-24 hours until cheese holds its shape.
Salt surfaces lightly. Transfer to aging cave at 50°F (10°C) and 95% humidity.
Wash rind with light brine every 2-3 days. Rind will turn orange-pink.
Age 6-10 weeks. Interior should become creamy near the rind.

notes: Named for Val Taleggio in the Bergamo Alps
Square shape is traditional and required for DOP status
Rind washing develops the characteristic pungent aroma
Interior is surprisingly mild compared to its strong smell

missing_inputs: as needed  brine solution for washing

recipes.title: Puzzone di Moena (Stinky Cheese of Moena)
recipes.source_note: Famously pungent washed-rind cheese from Trentino-Alto Adige.
recipes.description: Italy's stinkiest cheese from the Dolomite town of Moena. The name means 'big stinker' but the flavor is remarkably complex - earthy, meaty, with notes of hay and Alpine meadows.

instructions.text: Heat raw milk to 95°F (35°C). Add thermophilic starter and B. linens, ripen 45 minutes.
Add rennet and let set 35-45 minutes until firm break.
Cut curds into 1/2-inch cubes. Rest 5 minutes.
Slowly heat to 115°F (46°C) over 30 minutes while stirring gently.
Drain and press at 15 lbs for 30 minutes, flip, then 25 lbs for 12 hours.
Brine for 24 hours in saturated solution.
Age at 55°F (13°C) and 95% humidity. Wash rind with brine every 2 days for first month.
Continue aging 3-5 months, reducing washing to weekly. Rind becomes sticky and orange.

notes: Puzzone means 'big stinker' in local dialect
Traditional production uses milk from Rendena and Bruna cows
The smell is much stronger than the taste
Pairs wonderfully with polenta and speck

recipes.title: Grana Padano Tradizionale
recipes.source_note: DOP hard cheese from the Po Valley, Italy's most consumed cheese.
recipes.description: Grainy-textured hard cheese from the Po Valley, aged 9-24 months. Milder than Parmigiano-Reggiano with sweet, nutty flavors. Essential for risotto and pasta.

instructions.text: Allow whole milk to sit overnight. Skim cream from surface to create part-skim milk.
Heat to 91°F (33°C). Add starter and optional lysozyme, ripen 20 minutes.
Add calcium chloride, then rennet. Let set 15-20 minutes until firm break.
Cut curds into rice-sized grains - as small as possible.
Heat slowly to 131°F (55°C) over 45 minutes while stirring constantly.
Hold at 131°F for 30 minutes, stirring until curds are very firm and squeaky.
Let curds settle 45-60 minutes under whey. Collect in cheesecloth.
Press at 40 lbs for 2 hours, flip, 50 lbs for 24-48 hours.
Brine in saturated solution for 20-25 days, turning daily.
Age at 60°F (16°C) and 85% humidity for minimum 9 months, up to 24 months for Riserva.

notes: Grana means 'grainy' - referring to the texture
Part-skim milk is essential for proper aging
Originally created by Cistercian monks in 1135
More economical than Parmigiano-Reggiano with similar uses

recipes.title: Piave Vecchio (Aged Piave)
recipes.source_note: DOP hard cheese from the Piave River valley in Veneto.
recipes.description: Dense, intensely flavored aged cheese from the Dolomite foothills. Aged 12+ months, it develops crystalline texture and complex butterscotch notes. Often called the 'poor man's Parmigiano.'

instructions.text: Heat milk to 95°F (35°C). Add starter, ripen 30 minutes.
Add calcium chloride, then rennet. Let set 40 minutes until firm break.
Cut curds into 1/4-inch cubes. Rest 5 minutes.
Heat slowly to 118°F (48°C) over 40 minutes while stirring.
Continue stirring at 118°F until curds are very firm, about 30 minutes.
Drain and press at 30 lbs for 1 hour, flip, 45 lbs for 24 hours.
Brine in saturated solution for 3 days.
Age at 55°F (13°C) and 85% humidity for 12-18 months. Brush and turn weekly.

notes: Named for the Piave River that flows through Belluno province
Vecchio means aged 12+ months; Stravecchio is 18+ months
Develops tyrosine crystals like aged Parmesan
Excellent table cheese and for grating

recipes.title: Asiago Pressato (Fresh Asiago)
recipes.source_note: Fresh, mild Asiago from the Asiago Plateau in Veneto.
recipes.description: Young, mild Asiago aged only 20-40 days. Soft, springy texture with sweet, milky flavor. Quite different from the aged versions - this is a table cheese, not for grating.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 95°F (35°C). Add starter, ripen 20 minutes.
Add calcium chloride, then rennet. Let set 25-30 minutes.
Cut curds into 1/2-inch cubes. Rest 5 minutes.
Heat to 105°F (41°C) over 20 minutes while stirring gently.
Drain and press at 15 lbs for 30 minutes, flip, 20 lbs for 4-6 hours.
Brine for 12 hours.
Age at 50°F (10°C) for only 20-40 days.

notes: Pressato refers to the pressed fresh style
Much different from aged Asiago d'Allevo
Soft enough to slice for sandwiches
Popular as a table cheese in Northern Italy

recipes.title: Asiago Stravecchio (Extra-Aged Asiago)
recipes.source_note: Aged Asiago d'Allevo from the Veneto highlands, 15+ months old.
recipes.description: Intensely flavored aged Asiago, hard and crumbly with sharp, complex taste. Aged minimum 15 months for Stravecchio designation. Excellent for grating over pasta and risotto.

instructions.text: Skim cream from milk surface to create part-skim milk.
Heat to 95°F (35°C). Add starter, ripen 30 minutes.
Add calcium chloride, then rennet. Let set 30 minutes.
Cut curds into small 1/4-inch pieces. Rest 5 minutes.
Heat slowly to 115°F (46°C) over 30 minutes while stirring constantly.
Continue stirring at temperature until curds are very firm, about 30 minutes.
Drain and press at 25 lbs for 1 hour, flip, 35 lbs for 24 hours.
Brine for 4-5 days.
Age at 55°F (13°C) for minimum 15 months. Turn and brush weekly.

notes: Part-skim milk is essential for proper aging
Can substitute for Parmesan in many recipes

recipes.title: Provolone Valpadana DOP
recipes.source_note: DOP pasta filata cheese from the Po Valley, made since the 19th century.
recipes.description: Stretched-curd cheese from Northern Italy, available in Dolce (mild, 2-3 months) or Piccante (sharp, 4+ months) styles. Traditional shapes include salami, melon, and pear.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 97°F (36°C). Add starter and lipase (for Piccante style), ripen 45 minutes.
Add calcium chloride, then rennet. Let set 30-40 minutes until firm break.
Cut curds into 1/2-inch cubes. Rest 10 minutes.
Heat to 118°F (48°C) over 30 minutes while stirring.
Drain curds, let mat together for 2-3 hours until pH reaches 5.2-5.3.
Cut curd mass into strips. Place in 170-180°F (77-82°C) water.
Knead and stretch repeatedly until smooth and elastic. Form into desired shape.
Cool in cold water, then brine 24-48 hours depending on size.
Hang to age at 55°F (13°C). Dolce: 2-3 months. Piccante: 4-12 months.

notes: Valpadana refers to the Po Valley (Val Padana)
Traditional shapes hung by ropes for aging
Lipase gives Piccante version its sharp bite
Smoking is an option after initial aging

recipes.title: Burrata Pugliese (Apulian Burrata)
recipes.source_note: Fresh cheese from Puglia - mozzarella pouch filled with stracciatella and cream.
recipes.description: Luxurious fresh cheese from Puglia: a mozzarella shell encasing creamy stracciatella (shredded mozzarella curds mixed with cream). When cut, the rich filling oozes out.

instructions.text: Dissolve citric acid in 1/4 cup cool water. Add to cold milk.
Heat milk to 90°F (32°C) while stirring gently.
Add rennet diluted in water. Let set 10 minutes until clean break.
Cut curds into 1-inch cubes. Heat to 105°F (41°C).
Drain whey. Heat water to 175°F (80°C).
Add curds to hot water. Stretch until smooth and elastic.
Reserve 1/3 of mozzarella. Shred remainder into thin strands (stracciatella).
Mix stracciatella with cream and pinch of salt.
Form reserved mozzarella into thin pouches. Fill each with stracciatella mixture.
Pinch pouches closed. Store in salted whey. Eat within 48 hours.

notes: Burrata means 'buttered' - referring to the rich filling
Invented in Andria, Puglia in the 1920s
Must be eaten very fresh - within 2 days ideally

recipes.title: Stracciatella (Burrata Filling)
recipes.source_note: Creamy filling of shredded mozzarella curds and cream from Puglia.
recipes.description: The luscious filling inside burrata - shredded mozzarella curds soaked in fresh cream. Also served on its own as a luxurious fresh cheese.

instructions.text: Start with freshly made mozzarella curds, still warm from stretching.
Tear or shred the mozzarella into thin, irregular strands while still warm.
Place strands in a bowl. Add cream and salt.
Gently mix to coat all strands with cream.
Let rest 10 minutes for cream to be absorbed.
Serve immediately or use to fill burrata pouches.
Store in cream in refrigerator. Best within 24 hours.

notes: Stracciatella means 'little rags' - describing the shredded texture
The curds must be warm and fresh for proper texture
Can be served alone drizzled with olive oil
The same name as a soup and gelato - different preparations

recipes.title: Stracchino (Crescenza)
recipes.source_note: Ultra-creamy spreading cheese from Lombardy, also called Crescenza.
recipes.description: Extremely soft, spreadable cheese from Northern Italy. Mild, slightly tangy with a creamy, almost liquid texture when ripe. Perfect for focaccia and spreading.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 100°F (38°C). Add starter, ripen 30 minutes.
Add calcium chloride, then rennet. Let set 40 minutes until soft curd.
Cut curds into 1-inch cubes. Let rest 15 minutes.
Gently ladle curds into molds - do NOT press.
Drain at room temperature 12-24 hours, flipping every 4-6 hours.
Salt surfaces lightly.
Age at 50°F (10°C) for 1-3 weeks until very soft and spreadable.

notes: Stracchino comes from 'stracco' meaning tired - referring to tired cows returning from Alpine pastures
Crescenza is another name for the same cheese
Should be very soft, almost runny when ripe

recipes.title: Caciocavallo Silano DOP
recipes.source_note: Ancient pasta filata cheese from Southern Italy, DOP since 1996.
recipes.description: Pear-shaped stretched-curd cheese hung to age in pairs. The name means 'cheese on horseback' - tied in pairs that drape over a pole like saddlebags. Mild when young, sharp when aged.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 97°F (36°C). Add starter and optional lipase, ripen 45 minutes.
Add calcium chloride, then rennet. Let set 40 minutes until firm break.
Cut curds into 1/2-inch cubes. Rest 5 minutes.
Heat slowly to 115°F (46°C) over 30 minutes while stirring.
Drain curds, let acidify 4-8 hours until pH reaches 5.2.
Cut curd into strips. Place in 175°F (80°C) water.
Stretch and knead until very smooth. Form into pear shapes with small knob on top.
Tie pairs together at the knobs with twine. Cool in cold water.
Brine 8-12 hours. Hang over pole to age at 55°F (13°C) for 2-12 months.

notes: Ancient cheese predating mozzarella by centuries
Traditional to hang in pairs over a pole
Can be smoked after initial aging
Excellent grilled when aged - called Caciocavallo Impiccato

recipes.title: Scamorza Affumicata (Smoked Scamorza)
recipes.source_note: Smoked pasta filata cheese from Southern Italy.
recipes.description: Stretched-curd cheese shaped like a tied pouch, then smoked over hay or wood. Golden-brown exterior with smoky aroma and firm, slightly chewy texture. Excellent for grilling.

instructions.text: Dissolve citric acid in 1/4 cup water. Add to cold milk.
Heat milk to 90°F (32°C). Add rennet, let set 5-10 minutes.
Cut curds and heat to 105°F (41°C).
Drain whey. Let curds acidify 2-4 hours.
Heat water to 175°F (80°C). Stretch curds until smooth.
Form into pouch shapes, creating a 'neck' by pinching top. Tie with twine.
Brine 2-4 hours. Air dry 24 hours.
Cold smoke at 70-90°F (21-32°C) for 4-8 hours until golden.
Age 2-4 weeks at 55°F (13°C).

notes: Scamorza means 'beheaded' - referring to the pinched neck shape
Traditional smoking uses wheat straw or beechwood
Excellent melted on pizza or grilled as an appetizer

missing_inputs: as needed  wood chips for smoking

recipes.title: Fontina Val d'Aosta DOP
recipes.source_note: DOP Alpine cheese from the Aosta Valley since the 12th century.
recipes.description: Semi-soft Alpine cheese with earthy, nutty flavor and excellent melting properties. Made from milk of Valdostana cows grazing on Alpine meadows. Essential for fonduta (Italian fondue).

instructions.text: Heat milk to 97°F (36°C). Add both starter cultures, ripen 45 minutes.
Add calcium chloride, then rennet. Let set 35-40 minutes.
Cut curds into 1/2-inch cubes. Rest 5 minutes.
Heat slowly to 118°F (48°C) over 40 minutes while stirring gently.
Stir at temperature until curds firm, about 20 minutes.
Drain and press at 15 lbs for 30 min, flip, 30 lbs for 12 hours.
Brine for 12 hours.
Age at 50°F (10°C) and 95% humidity for 3-4 months. Wash and turn every 2-3 days.

notes: True Fontina DOP comes only from Val d'Aosta
Rind washing develops earthy, mushroomy notes
The foundation of classic Italian fonduta

recipes.title: Montasio Friulano DOP
recipes.source_note: DOP cheese from Friuli-Venezia Giulia, created by Benedictine monks.
recipes.description: Fruity, nutty cheese from the northeast corner of Italy. Ranges from soft and mild (2 months) to hard and sharp (12+ months). Essential ingredient for frico (crispy cheese wafers).

instructions.text: Heat milk to 90°F (32°C). Add starter, ripen 30 minutes.
Raise temperature to 95°F (35°C). Add calcium chloride, then rennet.
Let set 25-30 minutes until firm break. Cut into 1/4-inch cubes.
Heat slowly to 115°F (46°C) over 30 minutes while stirring.
Continue stirring until curds are firm, about 20 minutes more.
Drain and press at 20 lbs for 30 min, flip, 35 lbs for 12-24 hours.
Brine 24-48 hours depending on size.
Age at 55°F (13°C): Fresco (2-4 mo), Mezzano (5-10 mo), Stagionato (12+ mo).

notes: Named for Mount Montasio in the Julian Alps
Created by monks at Moggio Abbey around 1200 AD
Essential for frico - crispy cheese wafers from Friuli
Flavor ranges from mild and fruity to sharp and complex

recipes.title: Toma Piemontese DOP
recipes.source_note: Traditional Alpine cheese from the Piedmont region.
recipes.description: Rustic Alpine cheese from Piedmont with buttery, slightly tangy flavor. Semi-soft when young, firmer when aged. The everyday table cheese of the Piedmont mountains.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 90°F (32°C). Add starter, ripen 30 minutes.
Add calcium chloride, then rennet. Let set 40 minutes.
Cut curds into 1/2-inch cubes. Rest 5 minutes.
Heat gently to 100°F (38°C) over 20 minutes while stirring.
Drain and press at 10 lbs for 30 min, flip, 20 lbs for 8 hours.
Salt by rubbing surfaces or brief brining.
Age at 55°F (13°C) for 1-6 months. Turn weekly.

notes: Toma is a generic term for wheel-shaped Alpine cheeses
Part-skim version is traditional for longer aging
Rind may be rubbed with olive oil or tomato paste
Each valley has its own variation

recipes.title: Bitto Storico (Historic Bitto)
recipes.source_note: Ancient Alpine cheese from the Bitto Valley in Lombardy, unchanged for centuries.
recipes.description: Rare Alpine cheese made only during summer in high mountain pastures. Mixed cow and goat milk creates complex, grassy flavors. Can be aged up to 10 years.

instructions.text: Use fresh milk immediately after milking, still warm at body temperature.
Combine cow's and goat's milk. Add natural whey starter.
Add rennet. Let set 30-40 minutes at 95-100°F (35-38°C).
Break curds into rice-sized pieces using traditional spino tool.
Heat to 120-125°F (49-52°C) over 30 minutes while stirring constantly.
Let curds settle. Collect in linen cloth.
Press under increasing weight for 24 hours, flipping frequently.
Dry salt the surface daily for one week.
Age minimum 70 days, traditionally in stone caves. Can age 10+ years.

notes: True Bitto Storico made only in summer on mountain pastures
Must be made within 30 minutes of milking
Among the longest-aged cheeses in the world

missing_inputs: 1 cup natural whey starter (from previous batch)

recipes.title: Robiola Piemontese
recipes.source_note: Soft, creamy cheese from Piedmont, traditionally mixed milk.
recipes.description: Delicate, creamy cheese from Piedmont made from cow, sheep, and/or goat milk. Bloomy white rind develops with aging. Spreadable when young, runny when ripe.

ingredients.item: goat's milk (optional, for mixed milk version)

instructions.text: Combine milks if using mixed version. Heat to 72°F (22°C) - barely warm.
Add starter and P. candidum. Ripen 1 hour.
Add calcium chloride, then just 2 drops rennet. Stir gently.
Cover and let set at room temperature 18-24 hours until thick curd forms.
Gently ladle curds into small molds. Do not press.
Drain at room temperature 24-48 hours, flipping daily.
Salt surfaces. Age at 50-55°F (10-13°C) and 90% humidity for 1-4 weeks.
White mold will develop on surface. Ready when soft throughout.

notes: Traditional Robiola varies by specific valley and maker
Very little rennet - mostly acid-set cheese
Robiola di Roccaverano DOP is famous goat's milk version
Name may derive from Latin 'ruber' (red) or 'robur' (strength)

recipes.title: Caciotta alle Erbe (Herbed Caciotta)
recipes.source_note: Rustic Italian farmhouse cheese flavored with herbs.
recipes.description: Small, mild farmhouse cheese infused with Italian herbs. Caciotta is a generic term for small wheel cheeses made throughout central Italy, often flavored with local herbs.

instructions.text: Combine milks if using mixed version. Heat to 90°F (32°C).
Add starter, ripen 30 minutes.
Add calcium chloride, then rennet. Let set 40-45 minutes.
Cut curds into 1/2-inch cubes. Rest 5 minutes.
Heat gently to 100°F (38°C) over 20 minutes while stirring.
Add chopped herbs to curds, mix gently.
Drain and press at 10 lbs for 30 min, flip, 15 lbs for 4-6 hours.
Salt surfaces or brine briefly.
Age at 55°F (13°C) for 2-8 weeks.

notes: Caciotta means 'little cheese' - typically small wheels
Every region has its own version and herb combinations
Tuscany is particularly known for herbed caciotta
Can also be flavored with truffles, peppercorns, or chiles

recipes.title: Castelmagno d'Alpeggio DOP
recipes.source_note: Rare blue-veined cheese from mountain pastures in Piedmont.
recipes.description: Ancient crumbly cheese from Piedmont with subtle blue veining. Made in summer Alpine pastures, it develops complex, slightly spicy flavor with blue mold. Among Italy's most prized cheeses.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 95°F (35°C). Add starter (and P. roqueforti if not relying on natural molds), ripen 30 minutes.
Add rennet, let set 45-60 minutes until very firm curd.
Break curds into irregular pieces. Let drain in cloth 12-24 hours.
Break drained curd again. Mix with fresh curds from a second batch (traditional method).
Press mixture into molds at 15 lbs for 12 hours.
Salt surfaces. Age in natural cave at 50°F (10°C) and high humidity.
Blue mold develops naturally in cracks. Pierce if needed to encourage veining.
Age 2-6 months. Older wheels develop more blue and crumbly texture.

notes: One of Italy's oldest cheeses, documented since 1277
Traditional production mixes curds from two milkings
Blue mold develops naturally in aging caves
Best Castelmagno comes from summer Alpine pastures (Alpeggio)

recipes.title: Fiore Sardo DOP
recipes.source_note: Ancient Sardinian sheep's milk cheese, the original Pecorino.
recipes.description: Raw sheep's milk cheese from Sardinia, smoked over aromatic woods and aged 3-12 months. Sharp, complex flavor with smoky undertones. Sardinia's original cheese, predating Pecorino Romano.

ingredients.item: aromatic wood for smoking (oak, myrtle, or arbutus)

instructions.text: Heat raw sheep's milk to 95°F (35°C) - no starter culture traditionally used.
Add lamb rennet paste. Let set 40-60 minutes until firm break.
Break curds by hand into walnut-sized pieces.
Heat slowly to 104°F (40°C) while stirring gently.
Drain and press into molds by hand, forming wheel shape.
Press lightly for 6-8 hours, turning frequently.
Brine for 48 hours. Air dry 24 hours.
Cold smoke over aromatic woods for 10-15 days, several hours per day.
Age at 55°F (13°C) for 3-12 months. Rub with olive oil or sheep fat monthly.

notes: Fiore means 'flower' - from the thistle flower used in traditional rennet
Sardinia's original cheese, made for millennia by shepherds
Smoking was originally done in shepherd huts over cooking fires
Young Fiore Sardo is table cheese; aged is for grating

missing_inputs: as needed  aromatic wood for smoking (oak, myrtle, or arbutus)

recipes.title: Ragusano DOP
recipes.source_note: Ancient Sicilian pasta filata cheese, block-shaped and rope-aged.
recipes.description: Stretched-curd cheese from the Ragusa province of Sicily. Distinctive rectangular block shape, hung by ropes to age. Sweet and delicate when young, sharp and complex when aged.

instructions.text: Heat raw milk to 95°F (35°C). Add whey starter, ripen 30 minutes.
Add lamb rennet paste. Let set 60-90 minutes until very firm.
Break curds into small pieces. Let mature in warm whey 4-8 hours.
When curd stretches smoothly, cut into strips.
Place strips in 175°F (80°C) water. Stretch and knead extensively.
Form into rectangular block shape, traditional for Ragusano.
Brine for 24-48 hours.
Tie with rope and hang to age at 55-60°F (13-16°C) for 3-12 months.
Rub surface with olive oil and tomato paste mixture periodically.

notes: Traditional shape is a rectangular block (parallelepipedo)
Modicana breed cows give distinctive flavor
Surface is rubbed with olive oil and tomato paste
Block shape allowed easy transport on donkeys

recipes.title: Comté (Aged Alpine Cheese)
recipes.source_note: AOC/AOP cheese from the Jura mountains, France's most consumed cheese.
recipes.description: Noble Alpine cheese with extraordinary complexity - fruity, nutty, and caramel notes that develop over long aging. Made in large wheels from raw milk of Montbéliarde cows grazing on mountain pastures.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 90°F (32°C). Add thermophilic starter and P. shermanii, stir thoroughly.
Ripen for 30 minutes. Temperature should remain stable.
Add calcium chloride if using pasteurized milk. Add rennet diluted in cool water.
Let set 30-40 minutes until clean break forms.
Cut curds into tiny rice-sized pieces - this is critical for Comté's dense texture.
Begin stirring gently and slowly raise temperature to 130°F (55°C) over 45 minutes.
Hold at 130°F while stirring until curds are firm and squeaky, about 30 more minutes.
Drain curds into large cloth-lined mold. Press at 25 lbs for 30 minutes.
Flip and press at 40 lbs for 12 hours, then 50 lbs for another 12 hours.
Brine in saturated salt solution for 48 hours, flipping daily.
Age at 55°F (13°C) and 90% humidity for first month, rubbing with salt weekly.
Continue aging 8-24 months. Longer aging develops more intense flavor and crystalline texture.

notes: Traditional Comté is made from raw milk of Montbéliarde or Simmental cows
Small eyes develop from propionic fermentation during warm aging
Wheels traditionally weigh 80-100 lbs - scale recipe as needed
Crystals that form during long aging are tyrosine amino acid clusters

recipes.title: Reblochon (Semi-Soft Alpine Cheese)
recipes.source_note: AOP cheese from Haute-Savoie, essential for tartiflette.
recipes.description: Buttery, nutty washed-rind cheese with an ivory paste that becomes increasingly supple as it ripens. The name comes from 'reblocher' - to milk again - referring to the richer second milking.

ingredients.item: whole cow's milk (high fat content ideal)

instructions.text: Heat milk to 95°F (35°C). Add starter, P. candidum, and B. linens. Mix well.
Ripen for 30 minutes at stable temperature.
Add calcium chloride, then rennet diluted in water. Stir gently for 30 seconds.
Let set undisturbed for 45 minutes until soft curd forms.
Cut curds into 3/4-inch cubes. Let rest 10 minutes.
Gently stir for 20 minutes - do NOT heat further. Curds should remain soft.
Drain whey and ladle curds into small disc-shaped molds (traditional size ~5 inches diameter).
Allow to drain without pressing for 6-8 hours, flipping every 2 hours.
Salt all surfaces. Let rest overnight at room temperature.
Age at 55°F (13°C) and 95% humidity. Wash rind with light brine every 2-3 days.
Ready in 4-6 weeks when rind is orange-pink and interior is supple.

notes: Traditional Reblochon is made from raw milk of Abondance, Tarine, or Montbéliarde cows
The 'second milking' was historically richer in fat - use highest fat milk available
Fermier (farmstead) has green casein stamp; laitier (dairy) has red
Essential for authentic tartiflette - sliced over potatoes, lardons, and onions
Should smell like mushrooms and hazelnuts when properly aged

recipes.title: Tomme de Savoie (Rustic Mountain Cheese)
recipes.source_note: Rustic mountain cheese from the French Alps, traditionally made from skimmed milk.
recipes.description: Humble yet complex Alpine tomme with a thick gray-brown rind covered in yellow and orange mold patches. Semi-firm paste with nutty, grassy, earthy flavors and a slight tanginess.

ingredients.item: part-skim cow's milk (or skim evening + whole morning milk)

instructions.text: Heat milk to 90°F (32°C). Add starter culture and mix well.
Ripen for 45 minutes, maintaining temperature.
Add calcium chloride, then rennet diluted in water. Let set 45 minutes.
Cut curds into 1/2-inch cubes. Let rest 5 minutes.
Slowly raise temperature to 100°F (38°C) over 30 minutes while stirring gently.
Continue stirring at 100°F until curds shrink and firm slightly, about 20 minutes.
Drain curds and press at 10 lbs for 30 minutes.
Flip, press at 20 lbs for 6 hours, flip again, press at 20 lbs for 12 hours.
Dry salt all surfaces or brine for 12 hours.
Age at 55°F (13°C) and 90% humidity for 2-4 months.
Let natural rind develop - brush off excessive mold if needed but allow gray/brown coat to form.

notes: Historically made from leftover skimmed milk after cream was taken for butter
Lower fat content allows rustic rind to develop character
Natural rind should be left alone - it protects the cheese
Each wheel is unique due to wild ambient molds
Look for PGI label for authentic Tomme de Savoie

missing_inputs: 3 gallons part-skim cow's milk (or skim evening + whole morning milk)

recipes.title: Époisses (Washed Rind Cheese)
recipes.source_note: AOP cheese from Burgundy, washed with Marc de Bourgogne brandy.
recipes.description: The 'King of Cheeses' according to Brillat-Savarin. Intensely aromatic washed-rind cheese with a sunset-orange rind and spoonable creamy interior when perfectly ripe.

ingredients.item: Marc de Bourgogne or brandy (for wash)

instructions.text: Heat milk to 86°F (30°C). Add starter and B. linens, mix thoroughly.
Ripen for 1 hour at stable temperature.
Add calcium chloride, then rennet diluted in water. Stir briefly.
Let set undisturbed for 90 minutes until very soft curd forms.
Very gently ladle curds into small disc molds - do not break curds.
Drain naturally at room temperature for 48 hours, flipping 4-5 times.
Salt all surfaces. Rest at room temperature overnight.
Transfer to aging space at 55°F (13°C) and 95% humidity.
Mix Marc/brandy with water for wash. Wash rind every 2-3 days with this solution.
Continue washing and aging for 6-8 weeks until rind is deep orange and sticky.
When gently pressed, center should feel liquid. Ready when aroma is powerful but not ammonia.

notes: Brillat-Savarin called Époisses 'le roi des fromages' - the king of cheeses
Traditional wash is Marc de Bourgogne - grape pomace brandy
Banned on Paris Metro due to its powerful aroma
Best enjoyed at room temperature with Burgundy red wine
The orange color comes from B. linens bacteria, enhanced by the alcohol wash

recipes.title: Munster (Alsatian Washed Rind)
recipes.source_note: AOP cheese from Alsace and Lorraine, traditionally served with cumin.
recipes.description: Powerful Alsatian washed-rind cheese with orange-red sticky rind and supple, creamy interior. Strong barnyard aroma belies a surprisingly mild, earthy flavor.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 90°F (32°C). Add starter and B. linens, stir well.
Ripen for 45 minutes at stable temperature.
Add calcium chloride, then rennet diluted in water.
Let set 60-90 minutes until soft curd forms.
Cut curds into 1-inch cubes. Let rest 15 minutes.
Gently ladle curds into round molds (traditional size ~6 inches diameter).
Drain naturally 24-48 hours, flipping every 6-8 hours.
Salt all surfaces liberally.
Age at 55-60°F (13-16°C) and 95% humidity.
Wash rind with light salt brine every 2 days for first 2 weeks, then twice weekly.
Ready in 5-8 weeks when rind is orange-red and sticky. Serve with cumin seeds.

notes: Munster (French) vs Münster (German) - different spelling, same cheese tradition
Vosges mountain monks created this cheese in the 7th century
Traditionally served with boiled potatoes and cumin seeds
Smaller version called Géromé is also AOP
Aroma is much stronger than flavor - give it a chance!

recipes.title: Pont-l'Évêque (Washed Rind Norman)
recipes.source_note: AOP cheese from Normandy, one of France's oldest cheeses.
recipes.description: Square-shaped Norman washed-rind cheese with a golden-orange rind and soft, slightly springy interior. Milder than Livarot, with buttery, slightly tangy flavors.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 90°F (32°C). Add starter, B. linens, and P. candidum.
Ripen for 45 minutes, maintaining temperature.
Add calcium chloride, then rennet. Let set 60 minutes for soft curd.
Cut curds into 3/4-inch cubes. Rest 10 minutes.
Gently stir for 15 minutes without heating.
Ladle curds into square molds (traditional shape). Drain 24 hours, flipping frequently.
Salt all surfaces, including edges.
Age at 55°F (13°C) and 90-95% humidity.
Wash rind with light brine every 3-4 days.
Ready in 4-6 weeks when rind is golden-orange and interior springs back when pressed.

notes: Possibly France's oldest Norman cheese, mentioned in 13th century texts
Square shape distinguishes it from other Norman washed-rind cheeses
Milder than its stronger cousin, Livarot
The white P. candidum bloom should show through the orange wash
Best paired with Normandy cider or Calvados

recipes.title: Livarot (The Colonel)
recipes.source_note: AOP cheese from Normandy, nicknamed 'The Colonel' for its stripes.
recipes.description: Powerfully aromatic Norman washed-rind cheese wrapped with sedge grass bands. Deep orange rind encases a golden, oozy paste with meaty, complex flavors.

ingredients.item: sedge grass or raffia strips (for wrapping)

instructions.text: Heat milk to 86°F (30°C). Add starter and B. linens.
Ripen for 1 hour at stable temperature.
Add calcium chloride, then rennet. Let set 90 minutes for very soft curd.
Very gently ladle curds into cylindrical molds without cutting.
Drain naturally 48 hours, flipping every 8-12 hours.
Salt all surfaces liberally.
After 1 week, wrap with 5 strips of sedge grass or raffia around circumference.
Age at 55°F (13°C) and 95% humidity. Wash with salt brine every 2 days.
Continue washing and aging 6-8 weeks total.
Ready when rind is deep orange-red and center feels liquid when pressed.

notes: Nicknamed 'Le Colonel' for its five stripes resembling military rank
Stripes originally helped the soft cheese hold its shape
Traditional sedge grass (laîche) comes from Norman marshes
One of the strongest-smelling French cheeses
Historically food of the poor, now a protected delicacy

recipes.title: Langres (Washed Rind with Fontaine)
recipes.source_note: AOP cheese from Champagne with characteristic concave top.
recipes.description: Unique washed-rind cheese with a 'fontaine' (well) in the top, traditionally filled with Champagne or Marc. Orange-red wrinkled rind surrounds a creamy, intense paste.

ingredients.item: Marc de Champagne or Champagne (for finishing)

instructions.text: Heat milk to 90°F (32°C). Add starter and B. linens, mix well.
Ripen for 45 minutes at stable temperature.
Add calcium chloride, then rennet. Let set 75 minutes for soft curd.
Very gently ladle curds into cylindrical molds without stirring or cutting.
Drain naturally 36-48 hours, flipping every 8 hours. Do NOT flip after 48 hours.
Salt all surfaces except top - this creates the signature concave 'fontaine'.
Age at 55°F (13°C) and 95% humidity.
Wash sides and bottom with brine every 2-3 days. Never flip - top naturally sinks.
Age 5-8 weeks. The top depression should deepen as cheese ripens from outside in.
To serve traditionally, pour Marc de Champagne into the fontaine.

notes: The 'fontaine' (well) forms because the cheese is never flipped after molding
Traditional to fill the well with Marc de Champagne before serving
Wrinkled rind is characteristic - don't smooth it out
Related to Époisses but distinct AOP with different shape and process
The depression catches the alcohol and lets it seep into the paste

recipes.title: Morbier (Ash Line Cheese)
recipes.source_note: AOP cheese from Franche-Comté with distinctive ash line through center.
recipes.description: Semi-soft Jura cheese with a signature horizontal ash line through its center. Creamy, springy paste with fruity, slightly smoky flavor and an edible washed rind.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 95°F (35°C). Add both starters, mix well.
Ripen for 30 minutes at stable temperature.
Add calcium chloride, then rennet. Let set 45 minutes.
Cut curds into 1/2-inch cubes. Rest 5 minutes.
Slowly raise to 100°F (38°C) over 20 minutes while stirring gently.
Drain half the curds into mold and press lightly.
Sprinkle vegetable ash evenly over surface of pressed curds.
Add remaining curds on top. Press at 15 lbs for 6 hours, flip, 15 lbs for 12 hours.
Brine for 24 hours in saturated solution.
Age at 55°F (13°C) and 90% humidity for 2-3 months.
Rub rind with salt water weekly to develop thin washed rind.

notes: Ash line originally from wood ash protecting morning curd until evening milking
Today's ash is food-grade vegetable ash (vegetable carbon)
Mixed cultures give more complex flavor than single culture
The ash has no flavor - purely visual and traditional
Semi-soft paste should spring back when pressed

recipes.title: Saint-Nectaire (Rustic Auvergne Cheese)
recipes.source_note: AOP cheese from volcanic Auvergne region with distinctive rustic rind.
recipes.description: Rustic semi-soft cheese from Auvergne's volcanic soil, with a thick gray rind dotted with red, yellow, and white molds. Earthy, mushroomy paste with subtle hazelnut notes.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 90°F (32°C). Add starter, mix thoroughly.
Ripen for 45 minutes at stable temperature.
Add calcium chloride, then rennet. Let set 50 minutes.
Cut curds into 1/2-inch cubes. Rest 5 minutes.
Gently stir for 15 minutes without heating.
Press curds in mold: 10 lbs for 1 hour, flip, 15 lbs for 3 hours, flip, 20 lbs overnight.
Dry salt all surfaces or brine 6 hours per pound.
Age at 55°F (13°C) and 95% humidity on rye straw mats if available.
Turn daily for first week, then every 2-3 days.
Let natural molds develop - don't brush off. Ready in 5-8 weeks.

notes: Traditional aging on rye straw gives distinctive flavor and rind
Fermier version has oval green casein stamp; laitier has square
Volcanic soil of Auvergne gives milk unique mineral character
Multi-colored mold rind is desirable - shows proper cave aging
Named after Marshal of France who introduced it to Louis XIV

recipes.title: Cantal (Ancient Auvergne Cheese)
recipes.source_note: AOP cheese from Auvergne, possibly France's oldest cheese.
recipes.description: Ancient hard cheese from Auvergne with a distinctive two-day curd process. Firm, slightly crumbly paste with buttery tang that intensifies with age.

instructions.text: DAY 1: Heat milk to 90°F (32°C). Add starter, ripen 45 minutes.
Add calcium chloride, then rennet. Let set 45 minutes until firm curd.
Cut curds into 1/2-inch cubes. Let rest 5 minutes.
Stir gently for 30 minutes, maintaining 90°F.
Drain whey. Press curds at 10 lbs for 8 hours.
DAY 2: Break up pressed curd mass into walnut-sized pieces - this is 'tome fraîche'.
Mix salt thoroughly into broken curds. Let rest 1 hour.
Pack salted curds firmly into large cylindrical mold.
Press at 25 lbs for 24 hours, flipping every 6 hours.
Age at 50°F (10°C) and 95% humidity. Brush rind with salt water weekly.
Cantal Jeune: 1-2 months. Entre-Deux: 3-7 months. Vieux: 8+ months.

notes: Two-day process with 'tome fraîche' stage is unique to Cantal family
Tome fraîche is used fresh in aligot - mashed potatoes stretched with cheese
Three age designations: Jeune (mild), Entre-Deux (medium), Vieux (strong)
Pliny the Elder mentioned cheese from Auvergne in Roman times
Salers is closely related but made only from raw Salers cow milk

recipes.title: Ossau-Iraty (Basque Sheep Cheese)
recipes.source_note: AOP sheep's milk cheese from the French Basque Country and Béarn.
recipes.description: Firm sheep's milk cheese from the Pyrenees with nutty, slightly sweet flavor and hints of lanolin and grass. Dense, slightly crumbly paste with a natural brushed rind.

instructions.text: Heat sheep's milk to 86°F (30°C). Add starter, mix well.
Ripen for 45 minutes at stable temperature.
Add calcium chloride, then rennet (lamb rennet traditional). Let set 45 minutes.
Cut curds into 1/4-inch cubes - small for firm texture.
Slowly heat to 105°F (41°C) over 30 minutes while stirring.
Continue stirring at temperature until curds shrink and firm, about 20 minutes.
Drain and press at 15 lbs for 1 hour, flip, 25 lbs for 12 hours.
Brine for 24-48 hours in saturated solution.
Age at 55°F (13°C) and 85% humidity for 3-6 months.
Brush rind regularly to develop firm, natural coat.

notes: Made from Manech and Basco-Béarnaise sheep breeds
Name combines Ossau valley (Béarn) and Iraty forest (Basque)
Traditional with black cherry jam (cerises noires d'Itxassou)
Transhumance - seasonal mountain grazing - gives summer milk special character
Sheep's milk has higher fat and protein than cow's milk

recipes.title: Bleu d'Auvergne
recipes.source_note: AOP blue cheese from the volcanic Auvergne region.
recipes.description: Creamy, powerful blue cheese with ivory paste streaked with blue-green veins. Spicy, assertive flavor with mushroom and grassy notes from volcanic terroir.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 86°F (30°C). Add starter and P. roqueforti, mix thoroughly.
Ripen for 1 hour at stable temperature.
Add calcium chloride, then rennet. Let set 90 minutes for very soft curd.
Cut curds into 1-inch cubes. Let rest 15 minutes.
Very gently ladle curds into molds without pressing, layering salt between additions.
Drain naturally at room temperature for 3-4 days, flipping twice daily.
When firm enough, pierce with sterilized needle: 30-40 holes per side.
Age at 48-50°F (9-10°C) and 95% humidity.
Blue veins should develop within 2-3 weeks.
Ready in 4-8 weeks when extensively veined and creamy.

notes: Created in 1850s by Antoine Roussel using rye bread mold
Volcanic soil of Auvergne gives distinctive mineral notes
More assertive than Fourme d'Ambert, its milder cousin
Piercing is critical - creates air channels for mold growth
Pairs wonderfully with sweet wines like Sauternes

recipes.title: Fourme d'Ambert (Gentle Blue)
recipes.source_note: AOP blue cheese from Auvergne, one of France's mildest blues.
recipes.description: Tall cylindrical blue cheese with a dry gray rind and creamy ivory paste laced with delicate blue veins. Gentler than most blues with buttery, slightly sweet character.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 90°F (32°C). Add starter and P. roqueforti.
Ripen for 45 minutes at stable temperature.
Add calcium chloride, then rennet. Let set 75 minutes.
Cut curds into 3/4-inch cubes. Rest 10 minutes.
Gently ladle curds into tall cylindrical molds without pressing.
Drain naturally 2-3 days, flipping several times daily.
Dry salt all surfaces liberally.
Pierce with needle after 1 week: 20-30 holes per side.
Age at 48-50°F (9-10°C) and 90% humidity for 4-8 weeks.
Let gray natural rind develop. Interior should be creamy with delicate veining.

notes: One of France's oldest cheeses - possibly 2000+ years old
Milder than Bleu d'Auvergne due to less P. roqueforti and fewer piercings
Tall shape gives higher paste-to-rind ratio than flat wheels
Gray rind is characteristic - don't mistake for contamination
Excellent entry-level blue for those new to the style

recipes.title: Brillat-Savarin (Triple Cream)
recipes.source_note: Named after the famous gastronome Jean Anthelme Brillat-Savarin.
recipes.description: Luxuriously rich triple-cream cheese with 75% butterfat and a bloomy white rind. Buttery, tangy, and impossibly smooth - the ultimate indulgence.

instructions.text: Combine milk and cream. Heat to 72°F (22°C) - barely warm.
Add starter and P. candidum, stir gently.
Ripen for 30 minutes.
Add calcium chloride, then just 4 drops rennet diluted in water.
Let set at room temperature 18-24 hours until very thick curd forms.
Very gently ladle curds into molds - do NOT break curds.
Drain naturally 24-48 hours at room temperature, flipping gently 2-3 times.
Salt all surfaces very lightly.
Age at 55°F (13°C) and 90% humidity for 2-3 weeks.
White P. candidum bloom should fully cover surface when ready.

notes: Named after the author of 'The Physiology of Taste'
Triple cream = at least 75% butterfat in dry matter
Minimal rennet - mostly acid set for delicate texture
Best at room temperature when paste is spoonable
Created in the 1930s by Henri Androuët

recipes.title: Chaource (Bloomy Rind)
recipes.source_note: AOP cheese from Champagne with thick bloomy rind.
recipes.description: Tall cylindrical bloomy-rind cheese with a thick white P. candidum coat and a chalky-to-creamy interior. Mushroomy, slightly sour, with dense texture.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 90°F (32°C). Add starter and P. candidum.
Ripen for 45 minutes at stable temperature.
Add calcium chloride, then rennet. Let set 90 minutes for very soft curd.
Very gently ladle curds into tall cylindrical molds without cutting.
Drain naturally at room temperature 24-36 hours, flipping every 6-8 hours.
Salt all surfaces evenly.
Age at 55°F (13°C) and 90% humidity for 2-4 weeks.
Thick white bloom should develop within first week.
Young Chaource has chalky center; aged has fully creamy paste.

notes: From the town of Chaource in the Champagne region
Thicker and taller than Camembert with denser texture
Traditionally eaten young with chalky center still present
Pairs excellently with Champagne or Chablis
The thick rind is edible and flavorful

recipes.title: Saint-Marcellin
recipes.source_note: IGP cheese from Dauphiné, traditionally served in small terracotta crocks.
recipes.description: Small, delicate cheese that transforms from fresh and tangy to runny and complex. At peak ripeness, it becomes liquid gold that must be eaten with a spoon.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 72°F (22°C). Add starter, P. candidum, and G. candidum.
Ripen for 30 minutes.
Add just 3 drops rennet diluted in water. Stir briefly.
Let set at room temperature 24-36 hours until very thick.
Gently ladle into small (3-inch) molds without breaking curd.
Drain naturally 24-48 hours, flipping gently.
Salt very lightly all surfaces.
Age at 55°F (13°C) and 90% humidity.
When rind is wrinkled and cream-colored with blue-gray patches, cheese is ripening.
Eat from fresh to very ripe - flavor intensifies dramatically with age.

notes: Originally made with goat's milk, now typically cow's milk
Legend: saved Louis XI from a bear attack, became his favorite cheese
Traditionally sold in small terracotta crocks (coupelles)
At peak ripeness, entire interior becomes liquid
The wrinkled rind is normal and desirable

recipes.title: Valençay (Ash-Covered Pyramid)
recipes.source_note: AOP goat cheese with truncated pyramid shape covered in ash.
recipes.description: Striking truncated pyramid-shaped goat cheese covered in blue-gray vegetable ash. Firm, slightly crumbly paste with citrusy tang that develops complexity with age.

instructions.text: Heat goat's milk to 72°F (22°C). Add starter and P. candidum.
Ripen for 1 hour.
Add just 4 drops rennet diluted in water.
Let set at room temperature 18-24 hours until very thick curd.
Very gently ladle curds into truncated pyramid molds.
Drain naturally 36-48 hours until firm enough to unmold.
Salt all surfaces lightly.
Coat thoroughly with vegetable ash on all surfaces.
Age at 55°F (13°C) and 85% humidity for 2-5 weeks.
White mold will grow through ash, creating distinctive blue-gray appearance.

notes: Legend: Napoleon sliced top off full pyramid after Egyptian campaign defeat
More likely: flat top allows stacking during aging
Ash protects surface and neutralizes acidity for mold growth
Young: fresh and tangy; Aged: dense, nutty, complex
Loire Valley produces many famous ash-coated chèvres

recipes.title: Crottin de Chavignol (Aged Goat)
recipes.source_note: AOP goat cheese from Sancerre wine region, transforms dramatically with age.
recipes.description: Small barrel-shaped goat cheese that transforms from fresh and mild to hard and intensely goaty. The name means 'little dropping' - don't let that stop you!

instructions.text: Heat goat's milk to 70°F (21°C). Add starter, P. candidum, and G. candidum.
Ripen for 1 hour at stable temperature.
Add just 3 drops rennet diluted in water.
Let set at room temperature 24 hours until thick curd.
Gently ladle curds into small barrel-shaped molds (2-inch diameter).
Drain naturally 24-48 hours, flipping occasionally.
Salt all surfaces lightly.
Age at 55°F (13°C) and 80% humidity.
Track development: fresh (1 week), mi-sec (2-3 weeks), sec (5-6 weeks), très sec (10+ weeks).

notes: Name comes from oil lamp ('crot') shape - or possibly less savory origins
Four stages: fresh (white), mi-sec (some mold), sec (hard), très sec (rock hard)
Pairs perfectly with Sancerre wine from same region
Aged versions can be grated like Parmesan
Warmed crottin on salad is classic French bistro dish

recipes.title: Rocamadour (Tiny Goat Medallion)
recipes.source_note: AOP goat cheese from Quercy, one of France's smallest cheeses.
recipes.description: Tiny disc of goat cheese, just 1.5 oz, with intense flavor packed into a small package. Creamy when young, develops wrinkled rind and concentrated tang with age.

instructions.text: Heat goat's milk to 68-72°F (20-22°C). Add starter and G. candidum.
Ripen for 1 hour.
Add just 3 drops rennet diluted in water.
Let set at room temperature 24-36 hours for very thick, acidic curd.
Gently ladle curds into tiny (2-inch diameter, 1/2-inch tall) molds.
Drain naturally 24-36 hours. These tiny cheeses drain quickly.
Salt very lightly - tiny size means salt penetrates quickly.
Age at 55°F (13°C) and 80% humidity for 1-3 weeks.
Wrinkled cream-colored rind develops as it ages.

notes: Named after the pilgrimage town of Rocamadour in Quercy
Served as appetizer or dessert - often grilled on salad
High surface area to volume ratio = fast ripening

recipes.title: Banon (Chestnut Leaf Wrapped)
recipes.source_note: AOP cheese from Provence wrapped in chestnut leaves.
recipes.description: Unique Provençal cheese wrapped in chestnut leaves and tied with raffia. The leaves impart tannins that help ripen the interior to a runny, complex state.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 72°F (22°C). Add starter, mix well.
Ripen for 1 hour.
Add 4 drops rennet diluted in water.
Let set at room temperature 24 hours until thick curd.
Gently ladle into small round molds (3-inch diameter).
Drain naturally 24-48 hours until firm but still moist.
Salt lightly all surfaces.
Soak dried chestnut leaves in warm water or white wine/eau de vie until pliable.
Wrap each cheese in 4-5 overlapping leaves, tie with raffia in a cross pattern.
Age at 55°F (13°C) and 90% humidity for 2-4 weeks.
Leaves will brown; interior will become runny and complex.

notes: Chestnut leaves contribute tannins that transform the cheese
Traditional to dip leaves in eau de vie (brandy) before wrapping
Originally goat's milk, now cow's or mixed milk allowed for AOP
When opened, should be runny and aromatic
Autumn leaves harvested and stored for year-round production

recipes.title: Kasseri (Greek Pasta Filata Cheese)
recipes.source_note: Greece's signature stretched-curd cheese, similar to Italian provolone.
recipes.description: A pale yellow, medium-hard Greek cheese with a slightly tangy flavor. Made using the pasta filata (stretched curd) method, it melts beautifully and is essential for saganaki.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 95°F (35°C). Add starter culture and ripen for 45 minutes.
Add calcium chloride if using pasteurized milk. Add rennet and let set for 45 minutes until clean break.
Cut curds into 1/2-inch cubes. Let rest 5 minutes.
Slowly heat to 115°F (46°C) over 40 minutes while stirring gently.
Drain curds and let mat together for 30 minutes at room temperature.
Cut curd mass into strips. Place in 170°F (77°C) water until stretchy.
Knead and stretch until smooth and elastic. Form into balls or blocks.
Brine in saturated solution for 12-24 hours.
Age at 55°F (13°C) and 85% humidity for 2-4 months, rubbing with olive oil weekly.

notes: Kasseri means 'cheese' in Turkish, reflecting Ottoman influence
Traditional kasseri is made with sheep's milk or a sheep/goat blend
The stretching technique is key to its characteristic texture
Perfect for saganaki - fried cheese appetizer

recipes.title: Kefalotyri (Greek Hard Grating Cheese)
recipes.source_note: Greece's answer to Parmesan, a hard sheep's milk cheese for grating.
recipes.description: A hard, salty Greek cheese made from sheep's or goat's milk. Pale yellow with a sharp, tangy flavor, it's the traditional cheese for grating over pasta and for making saganaki.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 90°F (32°C). Add starter and ripen for 1 hour.
Add calcium chloride, then rennet. Let set 45-60 minutes until very firm break.
Cut curds into small 1/4-inch cubes.
Slowly heat to 120°F (49°C) over 45 minutes while stirring continuously.
Continue stirring at temperature until curds are very firm and squeak, about 30 minutes.
Drain and press at 30 lbs for 2 hours, flip, then 50 lbs for 24 hours.
Brine in saturated solution for 2-3 days, turning daily.
Age at 55°F (13°C) and 80% humidity for minimum 3 months, up to 1 year. Turn weekly.

notes: Kefalotyri means 'head cheese' referring to its round shape
Younger cheese is milder; aged version is sharp and crumbly
Essential for authentic Greek pasta dishes
Can substitute for Pecorino Romano in recipes

recipes.title: Graviera Kritis (Cretan Graviera)
recipes.source_note: PDO cheese from Crete, Greece's most popular table cheese.
recipes.description: A hard, pale yellow cheese from Crete with a sweet, nutty flavor reminiscent of Gruyère. Made primarily from sheep's milk with some goat's milk, it's aged in the island's unique climate.

instructions.text: Combine sheep's and goat's milk. Heat to 95°F (35°C).
Add starter culture and ripen for 30 minutes.
Add calcium chloride, then rennet. Let set 45 minutes until clean break.
Cut curds into 3/8-inch cubes. Rest 5 minutes.
Slowly heat to 122°F (50°C) over 45 minutes while stirring continuously.
Hold temperature and stir until curds are firm and shrunk, about 30 minutes.
Drain and press at 25 lbs for 1 hour, flip, then 45 lbs for 24 hours.
Brine in saturated solution for 2-3 days.
Age at 55°F (13°C) and 85% humidity for 5-12 months. Rub with olive oil monthly.

notes: Graviera is derived from Gruyère, brought to Greece by Swiss cheesemakers
Cretan version has PDO (Protected Designation of Origin) status
Sweet, fruity flavor with hints of burnt caramel
Greece's second most popular cheese after feta

recipes.title: Manouri (Greek Whey Cheese)
recipes.source_note: PDO whey cheese from Macedonia and Thessaly, Greece.
recipes.description: A soft, creamy Greek whey cheese made by adding milk or cream to the whey left over from feta production. Rich, buttery, and slightly sweet, it's often served with honey for dessert.

ingredients.item: fresh whey (from feta or other cheese)

instructions.text: Combine fresh whey, sheep's milk, and cream in a large pot.
Heat slowly to 195°F (90°C), stirring occasionally.
Add vinegar or lemon juice and stir gently.
When curds form and rise to surface, remove from heat.
Let rest 15 minutes for curds to consolidate.
Gently ladle curds into cheesecloth-lined molds.
Drain at room temperature for 24-48 hours without pressing.
Salt lightly and refrigerate. Best consumed within 1 week.

notes: Manouri is a byproduct of feta production - uses the leftover whey
Adding cream makes it richer than traditional whey cheeses
PDO protected - authentic manouri comes from Macedonia and Thessaly
Traditional dessert served with honey and walnuts

missing_inputs: 1 gallon fresh whey (from feta or other cheese)

recipes.title: Mizithra (Fresh Greek Whey Cheese)
recipes.source_note: Ancient Greek whey cheese, made fresh or aged.
recipes.description: A traditional Greek whey cheese available in two forms: fresh (soft and creamy) or aged (hard and salty for grating). The fresh version is sweet and ricotta-like, perfect for pastries.
recipes.total_time: 24 hours for fresh; 3-4 months for aged

ingredients.item: fresh whey (from feta or other sheep's milk cheese)

instructions.text: Combine fresh whey and sheep's milk in a pot.
Heat slowly to 190°F (88°C), stirring occasionally.
Add vinegar and stir gently once.
When white curds form and float to surface, remove from heat.
Let rest 10 minutes.
Skim curds into cheesecloth-lined colander.
Hang cheesecloth bundle to drain for 12-24 hours.
For fresh mizithra: Salt lightly and refrigerate. Use within 1 week.
For aged mizithra: Form into balls, salt heavily, and age at 55°F for 3-4 months until hard.

notes: One of the oldest Greek cheeses, mentioned in Homer's Odyssey
Fresh version is like Italian ricotta
Aged version (xinomizithra) is hard and used for grating
Essential for Greek pastries like kalitsounia

missing_inputs: 1 gallon fresh whey (from feta or other sheep's milk cheese)

recipes.title: Anthotyros (Fresh Greek Flower Cheese)
recipes.source_note: Delicate fresh whey cheese, named 'flower of cheese' for its lightness.
recipes.description: A fresh, soft Greek whey cheese with a delicate, slightly sweet flavor. The name means 'flower cheese' referring to its fine, light texture. Used in both savory dishes and desserts.

ingredients.item: fresh whey (from sheep's or goat's cheese)

instructions.text: Combine fresh whey and milk in a large pot.
Heat slowly to 185°F (85°C), stirring occasionally.
Add lemon juice and stir once gently.
Continue heating to 195°F (90°C) until fine curds form.
Remove from heat and let rest 10 minutes.
Carefully skim delicate curds with slotted spoon into cheesecloth.
Tie cheesecloth and hang to drain 12-24 hours.
Salt very lightly. Refrigerate and use within 5 days.

notes: Anthos means 'flower' - the finest part of the whey
Lighter and more delicate than mizithra
Can be made dry (xero anthotyros) for longer storage

missing_inputs: 1 gallon fresh whey (from sheep's or goat's cheese)

recipes.title: Kopanisti (Cycladic Spicy Fermented Cheese)
recipes.source_note: PDO spicy fermented cheese from the Cyclades islands, especially Mykonos.
recipes.description: A soft, pungent, spicy cheese from the Cyclades islands. Fermented for weeks until creamy and spreadable, it develops a distinctive sharp, peppery flavor. A beloved Greek meze.

ingredients.item: sheep's milk feta (or fresh sheep's cheese)

instructions.text: Crumble feta or fresh cheese into a bowl.
Mix in yogurt and half the olive oil until well combined.
Add salt and paprika, mix thoroughly.
Pack mixture tightly into a clay pot or jar.
Top with remaining olive oil to seal.
Cover and store at room temperature for 2-3 days.
Move to cool cellar or refrigerator. Ferment for 1-3 months.
Check weekly - mash and mix, adding olive oil as needed.
Ready when creamy, pungent, and spicy throughout.

notes: Kopanisti means 'beaten' from the repeated mashing
Mykonos version is most famous, has PDO protection
The longer fermentation, the spicier and more pungent
Serve as meze with bread or add to salads

missing_inputs: 2 lbs sheep's milk feta (or fresh sheep's cheese)

recipes.title: Katiki Domokou (Creamy Spreadable Cheese)
recipes.source_note: PDO fresh spreadable cheese from Domokos in Thessaly, Greece.
recipes.description: A soft, creamy, spreadable cheese from Thessaly with a tangy, refreshing flavor. Made from goat's or sheep's milk, it has a texture between yogurt and cream cheese. Perfect for spreading on bread.

instructions.text: Heat goat's milk to 185°F (85°C).
Cool to 110°F (43°C). Stir in yogurt.
Cover and let ferment at warm room temperature for 12-24 hours until thick.
Add lemon juice and stir gently.
Line colander with fine cheesecloth. Pour in mixture.
Drain at room temperature for 24-48 hours until creamy but spreadable.
Mix in salt. Transfer to container.
Refrigerate and use within 1 week.

notes: Texture should be creamy and spoonable, not firm
The tangy flavor comes from natural fermentation

recipes.title: Ladotyri Mytilinis (Lesbos Oil-Preserved Cheese)
recipes.source_note: PDO cheese from Lesbos (Mytilini), preserved in olive oil.
recipes.description: A hard, piquant cheese from the island of Lesbos, aged and preserved in olive oil. The oil gives it a unique smooth texture and rich flavor. One of Greece's most distinctive regional cheeses.

instructions.text: Heat sheep's milk to 95°F (35°C). Add starter and ripen 45 minutes.
Add calcium chloride, then rennet. Let set 45 minutes.
Cut curds into 1/2-inch cubes. Let rest 5 minutes.
Heat slowly to 110°F (43°C) over 30 minutes while stirring.
Drain and press at 20 lbs for 1 hour, flip, then 35 lbs for 12 hours.
Rub cheese generously with salt. Repeat daily for 1 week.
Air-dry at 55°F (13°C) for 2-3 weeks until rind forms.
Submerge cheese completely in olive oil in a crock or jar.
Age in oil at cool room temperature for 3-6 months.

notes: Ladotyri means 'oil cheese' - named for its preservation method
The olive oil both preserves and flavors the cheese
PDO protected - authentic version only from Lesbos
Oil becomes flavored and can be used for cooking

recipes.title: Formaella Arachovas Parnassou (Parnassus Mountain Cheese)
recipes.source_note: PDO cheese from Arachova on Mount Parnassus, Greece.
recipes.description: A semi-hard cheese from the village of Arachova on Mount Parnassus. Made from sheep's or goat's milk, it has a mild, slightly sweet flavor. Named for its small cylindrical 'formella' (mold) shape.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 90°F (32°C). Add starter and ripen 45 minutes.
Add calcium chloride, then rennet. Let set 45 minutes until clean break.
Cut curds into 1/2-inch cubes. Let rest 10 minutes.
Gently heat to 100°F (38°C) over 20 minutes while stirring.
Drain and ladle curds into small cylindrical molds (about 4 inches diameter).
Press lightly at 10 lbs for 2 hours, flip, then 15 lbs for 8 hours.
Brine for 12-24 hours depending on size.
Age at 55°F (13°C) and 85% humidity for 2-3 months.

notes: Traditionally made by shepherds on Mount Parnassus
Mild enough for everyday eating, firm enough for grilling

recipes.title: Sfela (Peloponnese Spicy Brined Cheese)
recipes.source_note: PDO cheese from Messinia and Lakonia in the Peloponnese, Greece.
recipes.description: A semi-hard, brined cheese from the southern Peloponnese with a distinctive spicy, peppery flavor. Often called 'the fire of Mani' for its sharp, aggressive taste. Made from sheep's and goat's milk.

instructions.text: Combine sheep's and goat's milk. Heat to 90°F (32°C).
Add starter and ripen for 1 hour.
Add calcium chloride, then rennet. Let set 45-60 minutes.
Cut curds into 3/4-inch cubes. Rest 10 minutes.
Gently stir curds for 30 minutes at 90°F (32°C).
Drain and press at 15 lbs for 2 hours, flip, then 25 lbs for 12 hours.
Cut cheese into thick slabs. Prepare heavy brine (7% salt minimum).
Submerge cheese slabs in brine. Store at 55°F (13°C).
Age in brine for minimum 3 months. Flavor intensifies with time.

notes: Sfela develops its spicy flavor from the aging process, not added spices
The sheep/goat milk blend is traditional to the Mani peninsula
PDO protected - only from Messinia and Lakonia regions
Much sharper and spicier than feta

missing_inputs: 1 lb per gallon water salt for brine

recipes.title: Metsovone (Greek Smoked Cheese)
recipes.source_note: PDO smoked pasta filata cheese from Metsovo in the Pindus Mountains.
recipes.description: A smoked, semi-hard cheese from the mountain village of Metsovo in Epirus. Made using the pasta filata method, then naturally smoked, giving it a distinctive smoky-sweet flavor unique among Greek cheeses.

instructions.text: Combine milks. Heat to 95°F (35°C). Add starter and ripen 45 minutes.
Add calcium chloride, then rennet. Let set 45 minutes.
Cut curds into 1/2-inch cubes. Rest 5 minutes.
Heat to 115°F (46°C) over 30 minutes while stirring.
Drain curds and let mat together for 2 hours until pH drops.
Cut curd mass into strips. Stretch in 170°F (77°C) water until elastic.
Form into oblong or cylindrical shapes. Brine 24 hours.
Dry surface for 2-3 days at 55°F (13°C).
Cold-smoke at under 90°F (32°C) for 2-4 days using aromatic hardwood.
Age at 55°F (13°C) for 3-4 months.

notes: Metsovo is a Vlach village known for its cheese tradition
PDO protected - only authentic if made in Metsovo region
The smoking uses aromatic mountain woods, traditionally beech

missing_inputs: as needed  aromatic hardwood for smoking (beech, oak)

recipes.title: San Michali (Syros Island Aged Cheese)
recipes.source_note: PDO hard cheese from the island of Syros, only Greek cheese from cow's milk with PDO.
recipes.description: A hard, aged cheese from the island of Syros, unique as Greece's only PDO cheese made exclusively from cow's milk. Sharp, granular, and perfect for grating, it reflects the island's Venetian heritage.

instructions.text: Heat cow's milk to 95°F (35°C). Add starter and ripen 45 minutes.
Add calcium chloride, then rennet. Let set 50 minutes until firm break.
Cut curds into small 1/4-inch cubes.
Heat slowly to 118°F (48°C) over 45 minutes while stirring continuously.
Hold temperature and stir until curds are very firm, about 30 minutes more.
Drain and press at 30 lbs for 2 hours, flip, then 45 lbs for 24 hours.
Brine in saturated solution for 2-3 days.
Age at 55°F (13°C) and 80% humidity for 8-12 months, turning weekly.

notes: Named after the patron saint of the village where it originated
Reflects Venetian and Italian influence on Syros island
Only Greek PDO cheese made exclusively from cow's milk
Similar in use to Parmesan or aged Pecorino

recipes.title: Kefalograviera (Hybrid Greek Hard Cheese)
recipes.source_note: A modern Greek cheese combining characteristics of kefalotyri and graviera.
recipes.description: A hard Greek cheese that combines the sharpness of kefalotyri with the sweetness of graviera. Light yellow with small holes, it's versatile for both table use and cooking, especially frying for saganaki.

instructions.text: Combine milks and heat to 92°F (33°C). Add starter and ripen 45 minutes.
Add calcium chloride, then rennet. Let set 45-50 minutes.
Cut curds into 3/8-inch cubes. Rest 5 minutes.
Heat slowly to 118°F (48°C) over 45 minutes while stirring.
Continue stirring until curds are firm, about 25 minutes more.
Drain and press at 25 lbs for 1 hour, flip, then 40 lbs for 12-24 hours.
Brine for 24-48 hours in saturated solution.
Age at 55°F (13°C) and 85% humidity for 3-8 months.

notes: A 20th century creation combining two classic Greek cheeses
The name literally combines kefalo- and -graviera
More approachable than pure kefalotyri, more complex than graviera
Excellent for saganaki due to high melting point

recipes.title: Emmentaler AOP (Real Swiss Cheese)
recipes.source_note: The original 'Swiss cheese' from the Emme Valley in Bern canton. AOP protected since 2006.
recipes.description: The authentic Swiss cheese with iconic large eyes, made with raw milk from grass-fed cows. Nutty, buttery, and slightly sweet - this is the real deal, not the processed imitation.

instructions.text: Heat raw milk to 90°F (32°C). Add thermophilic starter and Propionibacterium, ripen 20 minutes.
Raise temperature to 95°F (35°C). Add rennet diluted in water. Let set 30-40 minutes until firm break.
Cut curds into rice-sized pieces (1/8 inch) - tiny curds are essential for Emmentaler texture.
Heat slowly to 130°F (54°C) over 45-60 minutes while stirring constantly. This high cook is critical.
Hold at 130°F and stir until curds are very firm and squeak, about 45 minutes more.
Transfer curds under whey to large mold. Press at 30 lbs for 1 hour, flip, then 50 lbs for 24 hours.
Brine in saturated solution for 48 hours, turning halfway.
Age at 55°F (13°C) for 2-3 weeks, then move to warm room 68-72°F (20-22°C) for 4-8 weeks for eye development.
Return to 55°F cave for minimum 4 months, up to 12 months for full flavor development.

notes: True Emmentaler AOP must be made in specific Swiss regions with raw milk
Propionibacteria create CO2 during aging, forming the characteristic eyes
Traditional wheels weigh 170-220 lbs - scale up for authenticity
Eyes should be cherry-sized to walnut-sized, evenly distributed
No eyes = 'blind' cheese, indicates fermentation problems

recipes.title: Appenzeller (Herbed Brine Washed)
recipes.source_note: From the Appenzell region of northeastern Switzerland. Made for over 700 years with a secret herbal brine.
recipes.description: Switzerland's most aromatic cheese, washed with a secret herbal brine called 'Sulz' containing wine, spices, and 25+ herbs. Tangy, spicy, and complex with a distinctive orange rind.

instructions.text: Prepare herbal brine: Combine wine, vinegar, and herbs. Simmer 10 minutes, strain, add 2 tbsp salt. Cool and refrigerate.
Heat milk to 90°F (32°C). Add starter, ripen 30 minutes.
Add calcium chloride, then rennet. Let set 45 minutes.
Cut curds into 1/4-inch cubes. Rest 5 minutes.
Heat slowly to 118°F (48°C) over 40 minutes while stirring.
Hold at temperature and stir until curds shrink and firm, about 30 minutes.
Drain and press at 15 lbs for 30 min, flip, 30 lbs for 12 hours.
Brine in standard salt solution for 12 hours.
Age at 55°F (13°C) and 90% humidity. Wash rind with herbal brine every 2-3 days for first month, then weekly.
Age minimum 3 months (Classic), 4-6 months (Surchoix), or 6+ months (Extra).

notes: The real Sulz recipe is a closely guarded secret with 25+ herbs
This simplified version captures the spirit of the original
Classic = mild, Surchoix = medium, Extra = strong
The herbal brine gives Appenzeller its distinctive spicy kick
Orange rind develops from the wine and herb wash

recipes.title: Raclette du Valais (Traditional Melting Cheese)
recipes.source_note: From the Valais canton. Name comes from French 'racler' (to scrape). Medieval shepherds melted it by fire.
recipes.description: The ultimate melting cheese from the Swiss Alps. When heated, it becomes creamy and aromatic without separating. Traditionally scraped onto potatoes, pickles, and onions.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 90°F (32°C). Add starter, ripen 30 minutes.
Raise to 95°F (35°C). Add calcium chloride, then rennet. Let set 40 minutes.
Cut curds into 3/8-inch cubes. Rest 5 minutes.
Slowly heat to 105°F (40°C) over 30 minutes while stirring gently.
Continue stirring at 105°F until curds are firm but still moist, about 30 minutes.
Drain and press at 15 lbs for 30 min, flip, 25 lbs for 12 hours.
Brine in saturated solution for 24 hours.
Age at 55°F (13°C) and 95% humidity for 3-6 months.
Wash rind with light brine weekly to develop characteristic tan color.

notes: Lower cook temperature than Gruyere preserves more moisture for melting
Traditional raclette meal: melted cheese over boiled potatoes with cornichons and pickled onions
Half-wheel is traditionally held near fire, melted portion scraped onto plate
Modern raclette machines use small slices under heating element
Best melting cheese - stays creamy without separating

recipes.title: Sbrinz AOP (Extra-Hard Alpine Cheese)
recipes.source_note: Switzerland's oldest and hardest cheese, possibly predating Parmesan. Traded through Gotthard Pass for centuries.
recipes.description: Ancient Swiss grating cheese, harder than Parmesan. Intensely savory with crystalline texture. Traditionally broken into shards rather than cut, or shaved paper-thin with a Sbrinzhobel.

instructions.text: Heat raw milk to 90°F (32°C). Add starter, ripen 20 minutes.
Raise to 95°F (35°C). Add rennet. Let set 30 minutes until very firm break.
Cut curds into tiny rice-sized pieces. Rest 5 minutes.
Heat very slowly to 130°F (54°C) over 60 minutes while stirring constantly.
Hold at 130°F and stir vigorously until curds are extremely firm, about 45 minutes.
Drain and press immediately at 40 lbs for 1 hour, then 60 lbs for 24 hours.
Brine for 3-4 weeks, turning daily. This extended brining is unique to Sbrinz.
Age at 55°F (13°C) and 80% humidity for minimum 18 months, preferably 24-36 months.
Rub with olive oil monthly during aging.

notes: Sbrinz may be the ancestor of Italian grana cheeses
The extended brining (weeks vs hours) is unique to Sbrinz
So hard it's traditionally broken apart, not cut
Serve shaved thin or break into chunks for eating

recipes.title: Tête de Moine AOP (Shaved Rosettes)
recipes.source_note: Monastery cheese from Bellelay Abbey since 12th century. Name means 'monk's head' - shaved from the top like a tonsure.
recipes.description: Unique Swiss cheese traditionally shaved into delicate rosettes using a Girolle. The shaving releases aromatic compounds, intensifying flavor. Fruity, nutty, and elegant.

instructions.text: Heat raw milk to 90°F (32°C). Add starter, ripen 30 minutes.
Raise to 95°F (35°C). Add rennet. Let set 40 minutes.
Cut curds into 3/8-inch cubes. Rest 5 minutes.
Heat slowly to 118°F (48°C) over 40 minutes while stirring.
Stir at temperature until curds are firm, about 30 minutes.
Drain and press at 15 lbs for 30 min, flip, 30 lbs for 12 hours.
Brine for 12-18 hours.
Age at 55°F (13°C) and 90% humidity for minimum 75 days (3 months).
Wash rind with light brine every few days during first month.
To serve: Use a Girolle to shave into thin rosettes, or slice very thin.

notes: Named 'monk's head' because it's shaved from top like a tonsure
